title: Introduction to Asynchronous Messaging
bodyMd:
# 1. Introduction to Asynchronous Messaging ## Table of Contents - [1.1 Why Messaging Exists](#11-why-messaging-exists) - [1.2 Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication](#12-synchronous-vs-asynchronous-communication) - [1.3 Core Vocabulary](#13-core-vocabulary) - [1.4 Message Kinds: Command, Event, Query, Document](#14-message-kinds-command-event-query-document) - [1.5 Anatomy of a Message](#15-anatomy-of-a-message) - [1.6 The Two Fundamental Channel Types](#16-the-two-fundamental-channel-types) - [1.7 Coupling: What Messaging Removes and What It Doesn't](#17-coupling-what-messaging-removes-and-what-it-doesnt) - [1.8 The Costs of Going Asynchronous](#18-the-costs-of-going-asynchronous) - [1.9 Map of This Material](#19-map-of-this-material) - [1.10 Interview Talking Points](#110-interview-talking-points) --- > **Purpose:** Build the mental model and vocabulary that every later topic (message bus, event bus, brokers, RabbitMQ, Kafka) relies on. If you can explain *why* messaging exists and *what it costs*, the product details become easy. ```mermaid mindmap root((Async Messaging)) Why Decoupling Load leveling Resilience Scalability Vocabulary Producer / Consumer Broker Channel / Queue / Topic Message / Envelope Message kinds Command Event Query / Reply Document Channel types Point-to-point Publish-subscribe Costs Eventual consistency Duplicates Ordering Observability ``` --- ## 1.1 Why Messaging Exists In a system made of many services, components need to talk to each other. The simplest way is a direct call: service A calls service B over HTTP/gRPC and waits for the answer. That works — until it doesn't: | Problem with direct calls | What happens | How messaging helps | |---|---|---| | **Temporal coupling** | If B is down, A fails too | The message waits in a durable channel until B is back | | **Load spikes** | A burst of traffic overwhelms B | The queue absorbs the burst (*load leveling*); B drains at its own pace | | **Fan-out** | A must know and call every interested service (B, C, D…) | A publishes once; any number of subscribers receive it | | **Slow work in the request path** | User waits for email sending, PDF generation, etc. | Work is handed off and processed in the background | | **Cascading failures** | Timeouts propagate through call chains | Failures are isolated behind the channel | | **Scaling** | Hard to scale B independently of A | Add more consumers (*competing consumers*) | > **One-line definition:** *Asynchronous messaging is a way for software components to communicate by sending self-contained messages through an intermediary channel, without requiring the sender and receiver to be available at the same time.* --- ## 1.2 Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant A as Order Service participant B as Payment Service Note over A,B: Synchronous (request/response) A->>B: POST /payments B-->>A: 200 OK (A blocked while waiting) participant Q as Broker / Channel Note over A,Q: Asynchronous (fire and continue) A->>Q: publish ChargeCustomer Q-->>A: ack (stored) Q->>B: deliver ChargeCustomer (later, when B is ready) B-->>Q: ack (processed) ``` | Dimension | Synchronous (HTTP, gRPC) | Asynchronous (messaging) | |---|---|---| | Availability requirement | Both sides up at the same time | Only the channel must be up | | Latency of the caller | Waits for full processing | Returns as soon as the message is stored | | Result | Immediate response | Eventually, via reply message, event or polling | | Consistency model | Easier to reason about (immediate) | Eventual consistency | | Failure handling | Retries / circuit breakers in the caller | Redelivery, dead-letter queues, idempotent consumers | | Discoverability | Caller must know the callee's address | Caller knows only the channel (or nothing, in pub/sub) | | Debugging | Single stack trace / trace span | Distributed, needs correlation IDs and tracing | **Rule of thumb:** use synchronous calls when the caller *needs the answer to continue* (e.g. "is this password correct?"). Use messaging when the caller only needs to know the request was *accepted* (e.g. "send a confirmation email"). --- ## 1.3 Core Vocabulary | Term | Meaning | |---|---| | **Message** | A self-contained unit of data (headers + body) sent from one component to another | | **Producer / Publisher / Sender** | The component that creates and sends messages | | **Consumer / Subscriber / Receiver** | The component that receives and processes messages | | **Channel** | The logical pipe a message travels through (a queue, a topic, a subject, a stream) | | **Queue** | A channel where each message is delivered to **one** consumer (point-to-point) | | **Topic** | A channel where each message is delivered to **every** subscription (publish-subscribe) | | **Broker** | Server software that hosts channels, stores messages and delivers them (RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, Kafka…) | | **Routing** | Deciding which channel(s)/consumer(s) receive a message (by key, header, content…) | | **Acknowledgement (ack)** | Signal from consumer to broker: "I processed this, you may delete it" | | **Dead-letter queue (DLQ)** | Where messages go after repeated processing failures | | **Message bus** | An architectural layer (often a broker + conventions/library) that lets many applications exchange messages through a shared, uniform infrastructure | | **Event bus** | A publish-subscribe mechanism specialized in broadcasting **events** (facts that happened) to interested listeners — in-process or distributed | | **Event stream / log** | An append-only, replayable, ordered sequence of records (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar) | > **Watch out:** these words are used loosely in the industry. "Bus", "broker", "queue" and "topic" are often used interchangeably in conversation. In an interview, *define your terms first* — it signals seniority. --- ## 1.4 Message Kinds: Command, Event, Query, Document Not all messages mean the same thing. The **intent** of a message determines how it should be named, routed and handled. | Kind | Intent | Naming | Senders → Receivers | Can be rejected? | Example | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Command** | "Please do this" | Imperative verb | Many → **exactly one** logical handler | Yes (validation, business rules) | `ChargeCustomer`, `SendEmail` | | **Event** | "This happened" | Past tense | **One** owner → many (0..N) subscribers | No — it's a fact | `OrderPlaced`, `PaymentFailed` | | **Query / Request** | "Tell me something" | Question / Get… | One → one, expects a reply | N/A | `GetCustomerCreditLimit` | | **Reply** | Answer to a query/command | …Result / …Response | One → original requester | N/A | `CreditLimitResult` | | **Document** | "Here is some data" | Noun | Transfer of state, no implied action | N/A | `CustomerSnapshot` | ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Command["Command: one handler"] S1[Checkout API] -->|ChargeCustomer| H1[Payment Service] S2[Admin Tool] -->|ChargeCustomer| H1 end subgraph Event["Event: many subscribers"] P[Order Service] -->|OrderPlaced| E1[Inventory] P -->|OrderPlaced| E2[Email] P -->|OrderPlaced| E3[Analytics] end ``` **Why the distinction matters:** - A **command** has an owner on the *receiving* side (the Payment service owns `ChargeCustomer`). It is typically sent to a **queue**. - An **event** has an owner on the *sending* side (the Order service owns `OrderPlaced`). It is typically published to a **topic/exchange**, and the publisher does not know or care who listens. - Mixing them leads to "events" like `SendWelcomeEmailEvent` — which is really a command in disguise and re-introduces coupling. > This distinction is the seed of the **message bus vs event bus** comparison (see the dedicated file). --- ## 1.5 Anatomy of a Message ```json { "headers": { "messageId": "6b1d6a1e-6a2f-4f1b-9a63-1c3f1c2b6f10", "correlationId": "order-48213", "causationId": "3f6a2b77-0f0e-4a52-b6a1-6e4d1b3f8c22", "messageType": "Sales.Events.OrderPlaced.v2", "contentType": "application/json", "timestamp": "2026-10-11T09:31:04Z", "replyTo": null, "source": "order-service", "traceparent": "00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01" }, "body": { "orderId": "48213", "customerId": "c-991", "total": 129.90, "currency": "EUR" } } ``` | Header | Why it exists | |---|---| | `messageId` | Unique identity → enables **deduplication / idempotency** | | `correlationId` | Groups all messages belonging to one business flow / request | | `causationId` | The ID of the message that *caused* this one → builds a causal chain | | `messageType` | Lets the consumer pick a handler and deserializer; include a **version** | | `contentType` | Serialization format (JSON, Avro, Protobuf, MessagePack) | | `timestamp` | Ordering hints, TTL decisions, debugging | | `replyTo` | Address for the reply in request/reply | | `traceparent` | W3C trace context → distributed tracing across async hops | **Design guidelines for message bodies:** 1. Keep messages **small** — large payloads go to blob storage, the message carries a reference (*Claim Check* pattern). 2. Make messages **self-describing** — a consumer should not need to call back the producer to understand it (unless you deliberately choose *event notification*). 3. Treat the schema as a **public contract** — version it, evolve it backwards-compatibly. 4. Prefer **immutable** message types in code (records / readonly). --- ## 1.6 The Two Fundamental Channel Types Every messaging product, no matter how fancy, is built on two primitives. ### Point-to-Point (Queue) ```mermaid flowchart LR P1[Producer] --> Q[(Queue)] P2[Producer] --> Q Q --> C1[Consumer 1] Q --> C2[Consumer 2] Q --> C3[Consumer 3] style Q fill:#42A5F5,color:#fff ``` - Each message is processed by **exactly one** consumer instance. - Multiple consumers on one queue = **competing consumers** → horizontal scaling and load balancing. - Natural fit for **commands** and **work/job distribution**. ### Publish-Subscribe (Topic) ```mermaid flowchart LR P[Publisher] --> T{{Topic}} T --> S1[(Subscription A)] --> CA[Billing] T --> S2[(Subscription B)] --> CB[Shipping] T --> S3[(Subscription C)] --> CC[Analytics] style T fill:#EF5350,color:#fff ``` - Each message is delivered to **every subscription** (a copy per subscriber group). - Within one subscription, you can again have competing consumers. - Natural fit for **events** and broadcast notifications. > **Key insight:** Most real systems combine both: a topic fans out to one *queue per subscribing service*, and each service scales with competing consumers on its own queue. RabbitMQ (exchange → queues), Azure Service Bus (topic → subscriptions), AWS (SNS → SQS) and Kafka (topic → consumer groups) all implement this same shape. --- ## 1.7 Coupling: What Messaging Removes and What It Doesn't | Type of coupling | Removed by messaging? | Notes | |---|---|---| | **Temporal** (both must be up) | ✅ Yes | The broker stores messages | | **Location** (know the address) | ✅ Yes | Producers know only the channel name | | **Platform / language** | ✅ Mostly | As long as the serialization format is shared | | **Cardinality** (know how many receivers) | ✅ With pub/sub | Publisher is unaware of subscriber count | | **Schema / contract** | ❌ No | Consumers still depend on the message format — versioning is essential | | **Semantic** | ❌ No | Consumers still rely on what the message *means* | | **Broker** | ⚠️ Introduced | You now depend on the broker's availability and features | > Messaging trades **runtime coupling** for **contract coupling**. Senior engineers manage the contracts deliberately (schema registry, versioning rules, consumer-driven contract tests). --- ## 1.8 The Costs of Going Asynchronous Messaging is not free. Every one of these must be designed for: 1. **Eventual consistency** — after publishing `OrderPlaced`, the inventory isn't updated *yet*. UIs and APIs must tolerate that. 2. **Duplicates** — most brokers guarantee *at-least-once* delivery, so consumers must be **idempotent**. 3. **Ordering** — messages can arrive out of order (retries, parallel consumers, partitions). 4. **Poison messages** — a message that always fails can block a queue or loop forever without a DLQ. 5. **Dual-write problem** — "save to DB and publish" is not atomic without the **Transactional Outbox**. 6. **Observability** — a single user action becomes a graph of asynchronous hops; you need correlation IDs, tracing and queue-depth metrics. 7. **Operational overhead** — the broker is a critical, stateful piece of infrastructure (clustering, upgrades, monitoring, capacity). 8. **Harder testing** — end-to-end tests must wait for asynchronous effects. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Need to communicate between components] --> B{Does the caller need
the result to continue?} B -- Yes --> C[Synchronous call
HTTP / gRPC] B -- No --> D{Multiple independent
receivers?} D -- Yes --> E[Publish-subscribe
Event / Topic] D -- No --> F{Work can be
deferred or bursty?} F -- Yes --> G[Point-to-point queue
Command / Job] F -- No --> C ``` --- ## 1.9 Map of This Material | # | File | Focus | |---|---|---| | 1 | Introduction to Asynchronous Messaging | Vocabulary and mental models (this file) | | 2 | Message Bus Fundamentals | What a message bus is, topologies, how to use it, when to use it | | 3 | Messaging Patterns | Enterprise Integration Patterns used in practice | | 4 | Delivery Guarantees & Reliability | Acks, at-least-once, idempotency, ordering, outbox | | 5 | Message Broker Landscape | Kinds of brokers and the major products compared | | 6 | RabbitMQ Deep Dive | Exchanges, queues, bindings, reliability, operations | | 7 | Apache Kafka & Event Streaming | Log-based messaging, partitions, consumer groups | | 8 | Service Bus Frameworks | MassTransit, NServiceBus, Spring Cloud Stream, Dapr… | | 9 | Event Bus Fundamentals | In-process and distributed event buses | | 10 | Event-Driven Architecture Patterns | Notification, ECST, Event Sourcing, CQRS, Sagas | | 11 | Event Bus Products | EventBridge, Event Grid, Eventarc, in-process libraries | | 12 | Message Bus vs Event Bus | Differences and decision framework | | 13 | Interview Questions | Question bank and system design scenarios | --- ## 1.10 Interview Talking Points | Question | Strong answer in one breath | |---|---| | Why use messaging instead of HTTP? | To remove temporal coupling, absorb load spikes, fan out to many consumers and move slow work off the request path — at the cost of eventual consistency and operational complexity. | | Queue vs topic? | Queue = each message to one consumer (work distribution); topic = each message to every subscription (broadcast). Real systems combine them. | | Command vs event? | A command asks one owner to do something and may be rejected; an event states a fact owned by the publisher and can have zero or many subscribers. | | What does messaging *not* decouple? | The schema and semantics of messages — the contract. | | Biggest pitfalls? | Duplicates (need idempotency), ordering assumptions, poison messages (need DLQ), the dual-write problem (need outbox), and poor observability. |
keyConcepts: command vs event vs query messages
message envelope and headers (correlation, causation, trace context)
costs of async: eventual consistency, duplicates, ordering

title: Message Bus Fundamentals
bodyMd:
# 2. Message Bus Fundamentals ## Table of Contents - [2.1 What Is a Message Bus?](#21-what-is-a-message-bus) - [2.2 Message Bus vs Message Broker vs Message Queue](#22-message-bus-vs-message-broker-vs-message-queue) - [2.3 Architecture and Building Blocks](#23-architecture-and-building-blocks) - [2.4 Topologies: Hub-and-Spoke, Bus, Brokerless](#24-topologies-hub-and-spoke-bus-brokerless) - [2.5 Kinds of Message Buses](#25-kinds-of-message-buses) - [2.6 How to Use a Message Bus — Step by Step](#26-how-to-use-a-message-bus--step-by-step) - [2.7 Code Examples](#27-code-examples) - [2.8 When to Use a Message Bus](#28-when-to-use-a-message-bus) - [2.9 When NOT to Use a Message Bus](#29-when-not-to-use-a-message-bus) - [2.10 The Enterprise Service Bus (ESB) — and Why It Fell Out of Favor](#210-the-enterprise-service-bus-esb--and-why-it-fell-out-of-favor) - [2.11 Interview Talking Points](#211-interview-talking-points) --- > **Purpose:** Understand precisely what a "message bus" is, the pieces it is made of, how to introduce one into a system and — just as important — when it is the wrong tool. --- ## 2.1 What Is a Message Bus? A **message bus** is a shared communication infrastructure that lets multiple, independent applications exchange messages through a **common set of channels, a common message format and common conventions**, without connecting to each other directly. The name comes from the hardware **bus** in a computer: a single shared pathway that every device plugs into. Instead of wiring every component to every other component (N×(N−1) connections), each component plugs into the bus once (N connections). ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Before["Without a bus: point-to-point spaghetti"] A1[Orders] <--> B1[Billing] A1 <--> C1[Shipping] A1 <--> D1[CRM] B1 <--> C1 B1 <--> D1 C1 <--> D1 end subgraph After["With a message bus"] BUS[["Message Bus"]] A2[Orders] <--> BUS B2[Billing] <--> BUS C2[Shipping] <--> BUS D2[CRM] <--> BUS end style BUS fill:#42A5F5,color:#fff ``` In the *Enterprise Integration Patterns* book (Hohpe & Woolf), a Message Bus is defined by three things: 1. **A common communication infrastructure** — the channels (usually provided by a broker). 2. **A common data model / canonical format** — everyone agrees how messages look. 3. **A common command/event set** — everyone agrees what messages exist and what they mean. > **Practical definition:** In modern codebases, "message bus" usually means *a broker (RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, SQS/SNS, Kafka…) plus a client-side abstraction (MassTransit, NServiceBus, Spring Cloud Stream, Wolverine, Dapr…) that gives the application a uniform `Send` / `Publish` / `Handle` API, handles serialization, routing, retries, dead-lettering and observability.* --- ## 2.2 Message Bus vs Message Broker vs Message Queue These terms overlap; here is how to keep them apart. | Concept | Level | What it is | Examples | |---|---|---|---| | **Message queue** | Data structure / channel | A FIFO-ish buffer that holds messages until a consumer takes them | An SQS queue, a RabbitMQ queue | | **Message broker** | Server / product | Software that hosts queues/topics, stores messages, routes and delivers them | RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, Azure Service Bus, Kafka | | **Message bus** | Architectural pattern / layer | The overall shared messaging backbone + agreed formats and conventions; often a broker wrapped by a library | "Our MassTransit-on-RabbitMQ bus", NServiceBus, an ESB | | **Event bus** | Specialization | A bus focused on publish/subscribe of *events* | Guava EventBus, AWS EventBridge | ```mermaid flowchart LR APP[Application code] -->|Send / Publish / Handle| LIB[Bus abstraction
MassTransit, NServiceBus,
Spring Cloud Stream] LIB -->|AMQP / proprietary protocol| BRK[Broker
RabbitMQ, ASB, SQS] BRK --> Q1[(Queue)] BRK --> T1{{Topic / Exchange}} subgraph MB["The Message Bus = conventions + library + broker"] LIB BRK Q1 T1 end ``` **Interview phrasing:** *"A queue is a channel, a broker is the server that hosts channels, and a message bus is the architectural backbone — broker plus conventions — that lets all services communicate uniformly."* --- ## 2.3 Architecture and Building Blocks | Building block | Responsibility | |---|---| | **Endpoints** | Logical services connected to the bus; each has an input queue | | **Channels** | Queues (point-to-point) and topics/exchanges (pub/sub) | | **Routing** | Maps message types to destinations (by type, routing key, headers or content) | | **Serialization** | Converts objects ↔ bytes (JSON, Avro, Protobuf); usually with type metadata | | **Message envelope** | Headers: id, correlation, type, timestamps, trace context | | **Handlers** | Application code invoked per message type | | **Pipeline / middleware** | Cross-cutting concerns: logging, retries, validation, tracing, transactions, deduplication | | **Error handling** | Immediate retries, delayed (second-level) retries, dead-letter / error queues | | **Subscription management** | Who receives which events; created at startup or declared in infrastructure-as-code | | **Monitoring** | Queue depth, consumer lag, processing time, error rate, DLQ size | ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Producer["Producer endpoint"] PC[Business code] --> PS[Serializer] --> PO[Outbox / Transport] end PO --> X{{Exchange / Topic}} X -->|binding: OrderPlaced| IQ[(billing input queue)] IQ --> CP subgraph Consumer["Consumer endpoint"] CP[Transport] --> MW[Middleware:
tracing, retry, dedup] --> DS[Deserializer] --> H[OrderPlacedHandler] end MW -. after N failures .-> DLQ[(error / DLQ)] style X fill:#EF5350,color:#fff style DLQ fill:#757575,color:#fff ``` --- ## 2.4 Topologies: Hub-and-Spoke, Bus, Brokerless | Topology | Description | Pros | Cons | Examples | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Hub-and-spoke (centralized broker)** | All messages go through a central broker cluster | Simple to operate and secure, central routing | Broker is a critical dependency; possible bottleneck | RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, Azure Service Bus | | **Bus (distributed log / partitioned)** | Many broker nodes share partitions; clients talk to partition leaders | Massive horizontal scale, replay | More complex semantics (partitions, offsets) | Kafka, Pulsar | | **Brokerless (peer-to-peer)** | Library-level sockets, no central server | Ultra-low latency, no extra infra | No durability by default; you build reliability yourself | ZeroMQ, nanomsg | | **Managed / serverless** | Cloud provider runs the broker | No ops, pay-per-use, auto-scale | Vendor lock-in, quotas, less control | SQS/SNS, Google Pub/Sub, EventBridge | --- ## 2.5 Kinds of Message Buses ### By scope | Kind | Scope | Typical use | |---|---|---| | **In-process bus (mediator)** | Inside one application/process, in memory | Decouple handlers inside a monolith/modular monolith (MediatR, Wolverine local queues, Spring events) | | **Distributed message bus** | Across processes and machines via a broker | Microservices integration | | **Enterprise Service Bus (ESB)** | Organization-wide, with transformation/orchestration in the bus | Legacy enterprise integration (MuleSoft, IBM Integration Bus, BizTalk) | ### By delivery model | Kind | How it works | Products | |---|---|---| | **Queue-based (smart broker, dumb consumer)** | Broker tracks per-message state, deletes after ack, routes by rules | RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, SQS, Azure Service Bus | | **Log-based (dumb broker, smart consumer)** | Broker appends to a partitioned log; consumers track their own offsets; messages retained and replayable | Kafka, Pulsar, Kinesis, Redis Streams, Azure Event Hubs | | **Push-based event routers** | Broker pushes (often over HTTP/webhooks) to subscribers matching filters | AWS EventBridge, Azure Event Grid, Google Eventarc | | **Lightweight pub/sub** | Fire-and-forget, minimal persistence, very fast | NATS Core, Redis Pub/Sub, MQTT QoS 0 | ### By messaging style supported - **Send (command, 1:1)** — to a specific logical endpoint's queue. - **Publish (event, 1:N)** — to a topic; the bus routes to all subscribers. - **Request/Reply** — send with `replyTo` + `correlationId`, await response. - **Scheduled / deferred** — deliver at a future time (timeouts, reminders). --- ## 2.6 How to Use a Message Bus — Step by Step 1. **Identify the boundaries.** Which services own which data and capabilities? Messages flow *between* bounded contexts. 2. **Classify each interaction.** Command (1 owner, may fail), event (fact, N subscribers) or query (needs a reply — often better as sync HTTP/gRPC). 3. **Design message contracts.** Name them (`PlaceOrder`, `OrderPlaced`), define schemas, add versioning, put them in a shared contracts package or schema registry. 4. **Choose the broker and abstraction.** Based on throughput, ordering, replay needs, cloud, team skills (see the product files). 5. **Define the topology.** Queues per endpoint, topics/exchanges per event type, routing keys, DLQs. Prefer infrastructure-as-code or convention-based auto-provisioning. 6. **Make producers reliable.** Use publisher confirms, and the **Transactional Outbox** when publishing must be atomic with a DB write. 7. **Make consumers safe.** Idempotent handlers, manual acks *after* processing, bounded retries with backoff, DLQ, prefetch tuned. 8. **Add observability.** Correlation IDs, W3C trace context propagation, structured logs, metrics (queue depth, consumer lag, age of oldest message, DLQ count) and alerts. 9. **Plan for evolution.** Additive schema changes, tolerant readers, version in the message type, deprecation process. 10. **Test.** Unit test handlers in isolation; use in-memory transports or Testcontainers for integration tests; contract tests between producer and consumer. --- ## 2.7 Code Examples ### 2.7.1 A minimal in-process message bus (TypeScript) ```typescript type Handler = (message: T) => Promise; interface Message { readonly type: string; } class InMemoryBus { private commandHandlers = new Map>(); private eventHandlers = new Map[]>(); // Commands: exactly one handler registerCommand(type: string, handler: Handler) { if (this.commandHandlers.has(type)) throw new Error(`Handler already registered for ${type}`); this.commandHandlers.set(type, handler); } // Events: zero or many handlers subscribe(type: string, handler: Handler) { const list = this.eventHandlers.get(type) ?? []; list.push(handler); this.eventHandlers.set(type, list); } async send(command: T) { const handler = this.commandHandlers.get(command.type); if (!handler) throw new Error(`No handler for command ${command.type}`); await handler(command); } async publish(event: T) { const handlers = this.eventHandlers.get(event.type) ?? []; // Isolate failures so one subscriber cannot break the others await Promise.allSettled(handlers.map(h => h(event))); } } // Usage const bus = new InMemoryBus(); bus.registerCommand<{ type: 'PlaceOrder'; orderId: string }>('PlaceOrder', async cmd => { // ... persist order ... await bus.publish({ type: 'OrderPlaced', orderId: cmd.orderId }); }); bus.subscribe('OrderPlaced', async e => console.log('Send confirmation email', e)); bus.subscribe('OrderPlaced', async e => console.log('Reserve stock', e)); await bus.send({ type: 'PlaceOrder', orderId: '42' }); ``` ### 2.7.2 Distributed bus with MassTransit on RabbitMQ (C#) ```csharp // ── Contracts (shared package) ───────────────────────── public record SubmitOrder(Guid OrderId, string CustomerId, decimal Total); // command public record OrderSubmitted(Guid OrderId, DateTime SubmittedAt); // event // ── Configuration ────────────────────────────────────── builder.Services.AddMassTransit(x => { x.AddConsumer(); x.AddConsumer(); x.UsingRabbitMq((context, cfg) => { cfg.Host("localhost", "/", h => { h.Username("guest"); h.Password("guest"); }); // Retry policy applied to all endpoints cfg.UseMessageRetry(r => r.Exponential(5, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2))); cfg.ConfigureEndpoints(context); // convention-based queues, exchanges and bindings }); }); // ── Producer ─────────────────────────────────────────── public class OrdersController(ISendEndpointProvider send) : ControllerBase { [HttpPost] public async Task Post(SubmitOrder cmd) { var endpoint = await send.GetSendEndpoint(new Uri("queue:submit-order")); await endpoint.Send(cmd); return Accepted(); // 202: accepted for async processing } } // ── Command consumer (one logical owner) ─────────────── public class SubmitOrderConsumer(IOrderRepository repo) : IConsumer { public async Task Consume(ConsumeContext ctx) { await repo.Save(ctx.Message); await ctx.Publish(new OrderSubmitted(ctx.Message.OrderId, DateTime.UtcNow)); // event } } // ── Event consumer (one of many subscribers) ─────────── public class OrderSubmittedEmailConsumer : IConsumer { public Task Consume(ConsumeContext ctx) => Console.Out.WriteLineAsync($"Email for order {ctx.Message.OrderId}"); } ``` ### 2.7.3 Raw broker usage (Python, RabbitMQ via `pika`) ```python import json, pika conn = pika.BlockingConnection(pika.ConnectionParameters("localhost")) ch = conn.channel() ch.queue_declare(queue="submit-order", durable=True) ch.confirm_delivery() # publisher confirms ch.basic_publish( exchange="", # default exchange routes by queue name routing_key="submit-order", body=json.dumps({"orderId": "42", "total": 99.5}), properties=pika.BasicProperties( delivery_mode=pika.DeliveryMode.Persistent, content_type="application/json", message_id="b3c1...", ), ) def handle(ch, method, props, body): order = json.loads(body) try: process(order) # must be idempotent ch.basic_ack(delivery_tag=method.delivery_tag) except Exception: ch.basic_nack(delivery_tag=method.delivery_tag, requeue=False) # -> DLX if configured ch.basic_qos(prefetch_count=20) ch.basic_consume(queue="submit-order", on_message_callback=handle) ch.start_consuming() ``` > **Notice the difference:** with a raw client you hand-code acks, retries, serialization and topology. A bus framework turns this into conventions so every team does it the same way. --- ## 2.8 When to Use a Message Bus | Scenario | Why a bus fits | |---|---| | **Microservices that must stay independently deployable and available** | Removes temporal coupling between services | | **Background / long-running work** (emails, reports, video encoding, imports) | Offloads work from the request path; scales workers independently | | **Bursty traffic** (flash sales, batch uploads) | Queue absorbs spikes (load leveling) | | **Fan-out of business events** to many consumers | Publisher doesn't need to know subscribers | | **Long-running business processes** (order → payment → shipping) | Sagas / process managers coordinate via messages, survive restarts | | **Integrating heterogeneous systems** (legacy + cloud, different languages) | Common protocol and canonical message format | | **Reliable retries** for flaky downstream dependencies | Redelivery + backoff + DLQ instead of failing the user request | | **Modular monolith** (in-process bus) | Keeps modules decoupled now, makes later extraction into services easy | --- ## 2.9 When NOT to Use a Message Bus | Situation | Better choice | |---|---| | The caller needs an immediate answer (validation, read queries, auth) | Synchronous HTTP/gRPC | | A small app with a couple of components and a single DB | Direct method calls; maybe an in-process mediator | | Strong, immediate consistency across components is a hard requirement | A single transactional boundary (same DB/service) | | The team has no capacity to operate/monitor a broker | Managed service, or stay synchronous until needed | | You're only adding it "because microservices" | YAGNI — messaging adds failure modes | | Streaming analytics over large history with replay | A log-based platform (Kafka) rather than a classic queue-based bus | | Low-latency request/response inside one data center | gRPC; a bus adds latency and indirection | > **Senior signal:** "Distributed messaging buys availability and scalability with consistency and complexity. I introduce it where the decoupling pays for itself — usually at bounded-context boundaries and for background work — and keep synchronous calls for queries." --- ## 2.10 The Enterprise Service Bus (ESB) — and Why It Fell Out of Favor An **ESB** puts *logic* into the bus itself: message transformation, content-based routing, orchestration, protocol adaptation, sometimes business rules. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[CRM] --> ESB B[ERP] --> ESB C[Web Shop] --> ESB ESB[["ESB
transform, route,
orchestrate, adapt"]] --> D[Billing] ESB --> E[Warehouse] style ESB fill:#FFA726,color:#000 ``` | ESB promise | What often happened | |---|---| | Central place for integration logic | Became a bottleneck owned by one "integration team" | | Reuse through canonical models | Huge, slow-changing canonical schemas | | Orchestration in the bus | Business logic hidden in XML/config, hard to test and version | | One platform for everything | Expensive licenses, single point of failure | The microservices movement replaced it with the principle **"smart endpoints, dumb pipes"** (Martin Fowler / James Lewis): keep the bus a simple, reliable transport, and put business logic in the services. Modern message buses (MassTransit, NServiceBus, Kafka, cloud brokers) follow this principle. --- ## 2.11 Interview Talking Points | Question | Strong answer | |---|---| | What is a message bus? | A shared messaging backbone — channels plus common formats and conventions — that lets services communicate without direct connections. Usually a broker plus a client abstraction. | | Bus vs broker? | The broker is the server product; the bus is the architectural layer/pattern built on it (and can even be in-process). | | Why use a bus framework instead of the raw client? | It standardizes serialization, routing, retries, DLQs, outbox, sagas, tracing and testing across teams. | | When would you not use one? | When the caller needs a synchronous answer, the system is small, or strong immediate consistency is required. | | What was wrong with the ESB? | It centralized business logic and transformations in the pipe; modern systems prefer smart endpoints and dumb pipes. |
keyConcepts: message bus vs broker vs queue
bus building blocks: endpoints, routing, serialization, middleware
hub-and-spoke vs log-based vs brokerless topologies
how to introduce a message bus step by step
when to use and when not to use a message bus
Enterprise Service Bus and smart endpoints, dumb pipes

title: Messaging Patterns
bodyMd:
# 3. Messaging Patterns ## Table of Contents - [3.1 Pattern Map](#31-pattern-map) - [3.2 Channel Patterns](#32-channel-patterns) - [3.3 Consumer Patterns](#33-consumer-patterns) - [3.4 Routing Patterns](#34-routing-patterns) - [3.5 Message Construction Patterns](#35-message-construction-patterns) - [3.6 Error-Handling Patterns](#36-error-handling-patterns) - [3.7 Reliability Patterns: Outbox and Inbox](#37-reliability-patterns-outbox-and-inbox) - [3.8 Process Coordination: Sagas and Process Managers](#38-process-coordination-sagas-and-process-managers) - [3.9 Flow-Control Patterns](#39-flow-control-patterns) - [3.10 Pattern Selection Cheat Sheet](#310-pattern-selection-cheat-sheet) --- > **Purpose:** The Enterprise Integration Patterns (EIP) catalog (Hohpe & Woolf, 2003) is still the shared language for messaging. This file covers the patterns you will actually meet in RabbitMQ, Kafka, Azure Service Bus, SQS and bus frameworks — with when and why to use each. --- ## 3.1 Pattern Map ```mermaid mindmap root((Messaging Patterns)) Channels Point-to-Point Publish-Subscribe Dead Letter Channel Invalid Message Channel Consumers Competing Consumers Idempotent Receiver Selective Consumer Durable Subscriber Routing Content-Based Router Message Filter Splitter / Aggregator Recipient List Routing Slip Construction Command / Event / Document Request-Reply Correlation Identifier Claim Check Reliability Transactional Outbox Inbox Retry with Backoff Coordination Saga Process Manager ``` --- ## 3.2 Channel Patterns ### Point-to-Point Channel One message → one receiver. Use for commands and jobs. *(RabbitMQ queue, SQS queue, ASB queue.)* ### Publish-Subscribe Channel One message → a copy for every subscriber. Use for events. *(RabbitMQ fanout/topic exchange, SNS, ASB topic, Kafka topic with multiple consumer groups.)* ### Datatype Channel One channel per message type (`orders.order-placed`). Makes routing, permissions, monitoring and schema enforcement simple. Bus frameworks often create one exchange/topic per message type automatically. ### Dead Letter Channel (DLQ) Where the broker puts messages it **cannot deliver or process**: expired TTL, rejected without requeue, exceeded max delivery count, queue length overflow. ### Invalid Message Channel Where the *consumer* puts messages it can read but considers **invalid** (bad schema, failed validation). Separating it from the DLQ helps: invalid messages are a producer bug; DLQ messages may be transient failures. --- ## 3.3 Consumer Patterns ### Competing Consumers ```mermaid flowchart LR P[Producer] --> Q[(jobs queue)] Q --> W1[Worker 1] Q --> W2[Worker 2] Q --> W3[Worker 3] style Q fill:#42A5F5,color:#fff ``` - Multiple instances read the same queue; the broker hands each message to one of them. - **Scales throughput horizontally** and gives fault tolerance (a crashed worker's unacked messages are redelivered). - **Trade-off:** you lose global ordering. If order matters per entity, partition by key (Kafka partitions, ASB sessions, SQS FIFO message groups, RabbitMQ consistent-hash exchange / single-active-consumer). ### Idempotent Receiver A consumer that produces the same result whether a message is processed once or many times. **Mandatory** with at-least-once delivery. Techniques are detailed in the reliability file (dedup table, natural idempotency, conditional updates). ### Selective Consumer / Message Filter The consumer only takes messages matching criteria (headers, properties). Prefer broker-side filtering (bindings, subscription filters, EventBridge patterns) so unwanted messages never reach the consumer. ### Durable Subscriber A subscription that keeps receiving (storing) messages while the subscriber is offline. In RabbitMQ: a durable queue bound to the exchange; in Kafka: a consumer group with committed offsets; in ASB: a topic subscription. ### Polling vs Event-Driven Consumer | Style | How | Products | |---|---|---| | **Push (event-driven)** | Broker pushes to the consumer over an open connection | RabbitMQ `basic.consume`, ASB processor, NATS | | **Pull (polling)** | Consumer asks for batches | Kafka `poll()`, SQS `ReceiveMessage` (use long polling, up to 20 s), Pub/Sub pull | | **Push over HTTP** | Broker calls a webhook | Pub/Sub push, EventBridge targets, Event Grid | --- ## 3.4 Routing Patterns | Pattern | What it does | Implementation examples | |---|---|---| | **Content-Based Router** | Routes based on message content/headers | RabbitMQ topic/headers exchange, EventBridge rules, ASB SQL filters | | **Message Filter** | Drops messages that don't match | Subscription filters | | **Recipient List** | Sends to a computed list of destinations | Code in a router service | | **Splitter** | Splits one message into many (an order → one message per line item) | Consumer that publishes N messages | | **Aggregator** | Combines related messages into one (wait for all line items) | Stateful consumer keyed by correlation ID, with completion condition + timeout | | **Scatter-Gather** | Broadcast a request, aggregate replies (get quotes from N suppliers) | Pub/sub + aggregator | | **Routing Slip** | The message carries its own itinerary of steps | MassTransit Courier, workflow engines | | **Message Translator** | Converts between formats | Anti-corruption layer at a boundary | ```mermaid flowchart LR O[Order] --> SPL[Splitter] SPL --> L1[Line 1] --> PROC[Item processor] SPL --> L2[Line 2] --> PROC SPL --> L3[Line 3] --> PROC PROC --> AGG[Aggregator
by orderId] AGG --> DONE[OrderFulfilled] ``` --- ## 3.5 Message Construction Patterns ### Request-Reply over Messaging ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant R as Requester participant Q as request queue participant S as Replier participant RQ as reply queue (exclusive) R->>Q: GetPrice {correlationId: 7, replyTo: reply-q-abc} Q->>S: deliver S->>RQ: PriceResult {correlationId: 7} RQ->>R: deliver; match correlationId 7 ``` - The requester sets `replyTo` (a temporary or per-instance queue) and a `correlationId`. - RabbitMQ offers **Direct Reply-To** (`amq.rabbitmq.reply-to`) to avoid creating reply queues. - **Use sparingly** — it reintroduces temporal coupling. If you need an immediate answer, HTTP/gRPC is usually simpler. ### Correlation Identifier Every message in a business flow carries the same `correlationId`; each message also records its `causationId` (the message that triggered it). Essential for tracing, aggregators and sagas. ### Claim Check ```mermaid flowchart LR P[Producer] -->|1. upload 50 MB file| BLOB[(Blob storage)] P -->|2. message with blob URL| Q[(Queue)] Q --> C[Consumer] C -->|3. download by URL| BLOB ``` Brokers have size limits (SQS 256 KiB historically, raised to 1 MiB in 2025; ASB 256 KB Standard / up to 100 MB Premium; Kafka 1 MB default). Store the payload elsewhere and send a reference. ### Message Expiration (TTL) Set a time-to-live for messages that become worthless after a while (price quotes, OTP codes). Expired messages are dropped or dead-lettered. ### Message Sequence Large logical messages split into numbered chunks (`sequenceNumber`, `total`) and reassembled by the receiver. Prefer Claim Check when possible. --- ## 3.6 Error-Handling Patterns ### The retry ladder ```mermaid flowchart TD M[Message received] --> H{Handler succeeds?} H -- Yes --> ACK[Ack / commit] H -- No --> T{Transient error?} T -- No, permanent --> DLQ[(DLQ / error queue)] T -- Yes --> I{Immediate retries
left? e.g. 3} I -- Yes --> H I -- No --> D{Delayed retries left?
e.g. 10s, 1m, 10m} D -- Yes --> SCH[Schedule redelivery
delay queue / TTL+DLX] SCH --> H D -- No --> DLQ DLQ --> OPS[Alert, inspect, fix, replay] ``` | Technique | Purpose | |---|---| | **Immediate retries** | Handle blips (deadlock, brief network glitch) | | **Delayed / exponential backoff retries** | Give a failing dependency time to recover; add **jitter** to avoid thundering herds | | **Max delivery count** | Prevent infinite loops of poison messages | | **Dead-letter queue** | Park failed messages for inspection and replay | | **Error classification** | Don't retry permanent errors (validation, deserialization) — send straight to DLQ | | **Circuit breaker on consumers** | Pause consumption when a downstream dependency is down instead of burning retries | ### Poison message A message that fails every time (bad data, bug). Without a max delivery count it loops forever and, in ordered queues, **blocks everything behind it** (head-of-line blocking). Always configure a DLQ and alert on DLQ depth. ### DLQ operations checklist - Store the original message **plus** failure reason, exception, attempt count, original queue. - Provide tooling to **inspect, fix and replay** (move back to the original queue). - Alert on DLQ growth; treat a non-empty DLQ as an incident signal, not a trash can. --- ## 3.7 Reliability Patterns: Outbox and Inbox ### The dual-write problem ```csharp // ❌ Not atomic: the process can crash between the two lines await db.SaveChangesAsync(); // order saved await bus.Publish(new OrderPlaced()); // never sent → other services never learn about the order ``` Reversing the order is equally wrong: the event can be published for an order that then fails to save. ### Transactional Outbox ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant API as Order Service participant DB as Database participant R as Outbox Relay participant B as Broker API->>DB: BEGIN TX API->>DB: INSERT order API->>DB: INSERT outbox(message) API->>DB: COMMIT loop poll or CDC R->>DB: read unsent outbox rows R->>B: publish (with publisher confirms) R->>DB: mark sent end ``` - Business data and the outgoing message are written in **the same local transaction**. - A relay publishes outbox rows to the broker — by **polling** the table or via **Change Data Capture** (Debezium reading the DB log). - The relay can crash after publishing but before marking sent → **duplicates are possible**, so consumers must still be idempotent. - Built into MassTransit, NServiceBus, Wolverine, Brighter; Debezium has an Outbox Event Router. ```sql CREATE TABLE outbox ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY, aggregate_id VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL, type VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL, payload JSONB NOT NULL, occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), sent_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL ); CREATE INDEX ix_outbox_unsent ON outbox (occurred_at) WHERE sent_at IS NULL; ``` ### Inbox (Idempotent Consumer table) ```csharp public async Task Handle(OrderPlaced msg, MessageContext ctx) { await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(); // Unique constraint on (consumer, message_id) makes this the dedup gate var inserted = await db.Database.ExecuteSqlInterpolatedAsync( $"INSERT INTO inbox (consumer, message_id) VALUES ('billing', {ctx.MessageId}) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING"); if (inserted == 0) return; // already processed → skip await billing.CreateInvoice(msg.OrderId); // business effect await db.SaveChangesAsync(); await tx.CommitAsync(); // dedup record + effect commit together } ``` **Outbox + Inbox = effectively-once processing** on top of at-least-once delivery. --- ## 3.8 Process Coordination: Sagas and Process Managers A business process spanning several services cannot use one ACID transaction. A **saga** is a sequence of local transactions, each publishing a message that triggers the next; on failure, **compensating actions** undo previous steps. ### Choreography (event-driven, no coordinator) ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant O as Orders participant P as Payments participant I as Inventory participant S as Shipping O->>P: OrderPlaced P->>I: PaymentCaptured I->>S: StockReserved S-->>O: OrderShipped Note over I,O: On failure: StockUnavailable → Payments refunds → Orders cancels ``` ### Orchestration (central process manager) ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant SAGA as Order Saga (orchestrator) participant P as Payments participant I as Inventory participant S as Shipping SAGA->>P: CapturePayment (command) P-->>SAGA: PaymentCaptured SAGA->>I: ReserveStock (command) I-->>SAGA: StockUnavailable SAGA->>P: RefundPayment (compensation) P-->>SAGA: PaymentRefunded SAGA->>SAGA: mark order Cancelled ``` | | Choreography | Orchestration | |---|---|---| | Coupling | Services react to each other's events | Services know only the orchestrator's commands | | Visibility of the flow | Implicit, spread across services | Explicit, in one state machine | | Best for | Simple flows, 2–4 steps | Complex flows, timeouts, many branches | | Risk | "Event spaghetti", cyclic dependencies | Orchestrator becomes a god-service | | Tools | Plain pub/sub | MassTransit state machines, NServiceBus sagas, Temporal, AWS Step Functions, Camunda | Saga design rules: every step must be **idempotent**; compensations must be **retryable**; use **timeouts** (scheduled messages) for steps that never answer; store saga state durably with optimistic concurrency. --- ## 3.9 Flow-Control Patterns | Pattern | Purpose | Example | |---|---|---| | **Prefetch / QoS** | Limit unacked messages per consumer to balance load | RabbitMQ `basic.qos(prefetch=20)` | | **Backpressure** | Slow producers when consumers fall behind | Bounded queues (`x-max-length` + `reject-publish`), RabbitMQ flow control/memory alarms | | **Throttling / rate limiting** | Protect a downstream API with quotas | Concurrency limit per consumer, token bucket | | **Batching** | Improve throughput by processing in groups | Kafka `max.poll.records`, SQS batch receive (10) | | **Priority queue** | Urgent messages first | RabbitMQ priority queues (`x-max-priority`), separate queues per priority (usually better) | | **Delayed delivery** | Process later (reminders, retries) | ASB scheduled messages, SQS `DelaySeconds` (≤15 min), RabbitMQ delayed-message plugin | | **Message grouping / sessions** | Ordered processing per key with parallelism across keys | ASB sessions, SQS FIFO `MessageGroupId`, Kafka partition key | --- ## 3.10 Pattern Selection Cheat Sheet | Problem | Pattern | |---|---| | Scale out processing | Competing Consumers | | Notify many services of a fact | Publish-Subscribe | | Messages fail repeatedly | Max delivery count + Dead Letter Channel | | Duplicates from at-least-once delivery | Idempotent Receiver / Inbox | | DB write and publish must be atomic | Transactional Outbox | | Large payloads | Claim Check | | Track a flow across services | Correlation Identifier + tracing | | Multi-service business transaction | Saga (choreography or orchestration) | | Ordered processing per entity | Partition key / session / message group | | Protect slow downstream | Prefetch, throttling, circuit breaker | | Get an answer asynchronously | Request-Reply (or prefer sync call) | | Combine N related messages | Aggregator with timeout |
