title: Delivery Guarantees & Reliability
bodyMd:
# 4. Delivery Guarantees & Reliability ## Table of Contents - [4.1 Where Messages Get Lost or Duplicated](#41-where-messages-get-lost-or-duplicated) - [4.2 The Three Delivery Semantics](#42-the-three-delivery-semantics) - [4.3 Producer-Side Reliability](#43-producer-side-reliability) - [4.4 Broker-Side Durability](#44-broker-side-durability) - [4.5 Consumer-Side Reliability: Acknowledgements](#45-consumer-side-reliability-acknowledgements) - [4.6 Idempotency Techniques](#46-idempotency-techniques) - [4.7 Exactly-Once: Myth, Marketing and Reality](#47-exactly-once-myth-marketing-and-reality) - [4.8 Message Ordering](#48-message-ordering) - [4.9 Schema Evolution and Versioning](#49-schema-evolution-and-versioning) - [4.10 Observability for Messaging](#410-observability-for-messaging) - [4.11 Security](#411-security) - [4.12 Interview Talking Points](#412-interview-talking-points) --- > **Purpose:** The hardest interview questions about messaging are about guarantees: *"Can this message be lost? Processed twice? Out of order?"* This file gives you precise answers. --- ## 4.1 Where Messages Get Lost or Duplicated ```mermaid flowchart LR P[Producer] -->|"① network fails before broker stores it
② broker stores, ack lost → producer retries → duplicate"| B[(Broker)] B -->|"③ broker crashes before fsync/replication → loss"| B B -->|"④ delivered, consumer crashes before ack → redelivery → duplicate
⑤ auto-ack before processing, consumer crashes → loss"| C[Consumer] C -->|"⑥ side effect done, ack fails → redelivery → duplicate"| DB[(Side effects)] ``` There are **three hops** where something can go wrong: producer → broker, inside the broker, broker → consumer. Each guarantee you claim must cover all three. --- ## 4.2 The Three Delivery Semantics | Semantics | Meaning | How it's achieved | Risk | Use for | |---|---|---|---|---| | **At-most-once** | Delivered 0 or 1 times | Fire-and-forget publish; ack *before* processing (auto-ack) | **Loss** | Metrics, telemetry, presence, live prices | | **At-least-once** | Delivered 1 or more times | Producer retries until confirmed; consumer acks *after* processing | **Duplicates** | The default for business messages | | **Exactly-once** | Effect happens exactly once | At-least-once + deduplication/idempotency, or transactional systems (Kafka EOS within Kafka) | Complexity, scope limits | Payments, ledgers, counters | > **Golden rule:** design for **at-least-once delivery + idempotent consumers**. That combination gives you *effectively-once processing* and works on every broker. --- ## 4.3 Producer-Side Reliability | Mechanism | What it does | Products | |---|---|---| | **Publisher confirms / acks** | Broker confirms the message is stored (and replicated) | RabbitMQ publisher confirms; Kafka `acks=all`; SQS/ASB/Pub/Sub return success on send | | **Retries with backoff** | Resend when no confirmation | All clients | | **Idempotent producer** | Broker deduplicates producer retries | Kafka `enable.idempotence=true` (default since Kafka 3.0); SQS FIFO dedup ID; ASB duplicate detection; NATS JetStream `Nats-Msg-Id` | | **Mandatory flag / unroutable handling** | Detect messages that matched no queue | RabbitMQ `mandatory` + `basic.return`, alternate exchange | | **Transactional Outbox** | Atomic DB write + publish intent | Framework feature or Debezium CDC | | **Local buffering** | Survive brief broker outages | Kafka producer buffer, client-side outbox | ```java // Kafka producer configured for durability Properties props = new Properties(); props.put(ProducerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "kafka:9092"); props.put(ProducerConfig.ACKS_CONFIG, "all"); // wait for all in-sync replicas props.put(ProducerConfig.ENABLE_IDEMPOTENCE_CONFIG, "true"); // no duplicates from retries props.put(ProducerConfig.RETRIES_CONFIG, Integer.MAX_VALUE); props.put(ProducerConfig.DELIVERY_TIMEOUT_MS_CONFIG, 120_000); ``` --- ## 4.4 Broker-Side Durability | Concern | RabbitMQ | Kafka | Cloud managed | |---|---|---|---| | Survive broker restart | Durable queue + persistent messages | Always on disk (log segments) | Built in | | Survive node loss | **Quorum queues** (Raft replication) | Replication factor ≥ 3, `min.insync.replicas=2` | Multi-AZ by default (SQS, ASB Premium, Pub/Sub) | | Retention after consumption | Deleted on ack (streams retain) | Retained by time/size, independent of consumption | SQS: until deleted (max 14 days); Pub/Sub: configurable | > **Durability costs latency.** fsync and replication add milliseconds. That's why at-most-once telemetry pipelines skip them. --- ## 4.5 Consumer-Side Reliability: Acknowledgements ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant B as Broker participant C as Consumer participant DB as Database B->>C: deliver msg (unacked, invisible to others) C->>DB: process + commit alt success C->>B: ack → message deleted else failure C->>B: nack / reject (requeue or dead-letter) else consumer crashes / times out B->>B: connection lost or visibility timeout expires B->>C: redeliver (to this or another consumer) end ``` | Product | Ack model | Redelivery trigger | |---|---|---| | RabbitMQ | `basic.ack` / `basic.nack` / `basic.reject` per delivery tag | Channel/connection closes with unacked messages; consumer ack timeout (default 30 min) | | Kafka | Commit the **offset** (position) per partition | Consumer restarts from last committed offset — everything after it is reprocessed | | SQS | `DeleteMessage` with receipt handle | **Visibility timeout** expires (default 30 s, max 12 h) | | Azure Service Bus | Peek-lock: `Complete` / `Abandon` / `DeadLetter` / `Defer` | Lock expires; `MaxDeliveryCount` (default 10) → DLQ | | Google Pub/Sub | `ack` / `nack` | Ack deadline expires | **Rules:** 1. **Ack after the side effect is durable**, never before (unless you deliberately want at-most-once). 2. If processing can exceed the lock/visibility timeout, **extend it** (heartbeat / lock renewal) or the message will be redelivered while you're still working on it. 3. With Kafka, **commit offsets after processing**; auto-commit can commit before processing completes → loss on crash. --- ## 4.6 Idempotency Techniques | Technique | How | Example | |---|---|---| | **Naturally idempotent operation** | Operation gives the same result when repeated | `SET status = 'Shipped'`, upsert, `PUT` | | **Deduplication store (inbox)** | Record processed message IDs with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the effect | `INSERT INTO inbox(message_id) ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` | | **Business key uniqueness** | Unique constraint on the business identifier | One invoice per `order_id` | | **Conditional / versioned update** | Apply only if the version matches | `UPDATE account SET balance = ?, version = 8 WHERE id = ? AND version = 7` | | **Idempotency key to downstream APIs** | Pass the message ID to external APIs that support it | Stripe `Idempotency-Key` header | | **Event sequence numbers** | Ignore events older than the last applied | Projection stores `last_event_number` per aggregate | ```python def handle_payment_captured(msg, conn): with conn.transaction(): inserted = conn.execute( "INSERT INTO processed_messages (consumer, message_id) VALUES (%s, %s) " "ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING", ("ledger", msg.id)).rowcount if inserted == 0: return # duplicate — already applied conn.execute( "INSERT INTO ledger_entries (order_id, amount) VALUES (%s, %s)", (msg.order_id, msg.amount)) ``` > **Pitfall:** checking `if not exists(messageId)` and inserting later, in separate transactions, is a race condition. The dedup record and the effect must commit **atomically**, enforced by a unique constraint. Dedup tables also need a retention/cleanup policy. --- ## 4.7 Exactly-Once: Myth, Marketing and Reality - In a distributed system with failures, **exactly-once *delivery* is impossible** in general (Two Generals problem): the sender can never be sure the ack wasn't lost. - What products offer is **exactly-once *processing* within a bounded scope**: | Offering | Real scope | |---|---| | **Kafka EOS** (idempotent producer + transactions + `isolation.level=read_committed`) | Read-process-write **within Kafka** (consume from topic A, produce to topic B, commit offsets atomically). Side effects in external DBs are not covered. | | **SQS FIFO** | Deduplicates messages with the same dedup ID **within a 5-minute window** | | **Azure Service Bus duplicate detection** | Deduplicates by `MessageId` within a configurable window | | **Google Pub/Sub exactly-once delivery** | For pull subscriptions in a region, acked messages aren't redelivered — consumer must still handle ack failures | **Interview answer:** *"Exactly-once delivery isn't achievable end-to-end; we get effectively-once processing by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers, and an outbox on the producer side."* --- ## 4.8 Message Ordering ### Why order breaks - **Competing consumers** process in parallel; message 2 can finish before message 1. - **Retries / redelivery** put a failed message back after later ones. - **Multiple producers** have no global clock. - **Partitioned systems** order only within a partition. ### Ordering strategies | Strategy | How | Products | |---|---|---| | **Per-key ordering via partitioning** | All messages for one entity go to the same partition/group; parallelism across keys | Kafka partition key, SQS FIFO `MessageGroupId`, ASB sessions, Pub/Sub ordering keys, RabbitMQ consistent-hash exchange or single active consumer | | **Single consumer** | One consumer per queue | RabbitMQ single active consumer (failover) — limits throughput | | **Sequence numbers + resequencer** | Consumer buffers and reorders | Custom, adds latency | | **Make order irrelevant** | Design commutative/idempotent operations, or carry version numbers and discard stale updates | Best option when possible | ```mermaid flowchart LR P[Producer] -->|key=customer-1| P0[Partition 0] P -->|key=customer-2| P1[Partition 1] P -->|key=customer-1| P0 P0 --> C0[Consumer A
ordered for customer-1] P1 --> C1[Consumer B
ordered for customer-2] ``` > **Ask in interviews:** "Do we need *global* order or *per-entity* order?" Global order means a single partition/consumer and kills scalability; per-entity order is almost always what the business actually needs. --- ## 4.9 Schema Evolution and Versioning Messages outlive deployments: producers and consumers are upgraded at different times, and old messages may still sit in queues or logs. | Change | Backward compatible? | Notes | |---|---|---| | Add an optional field | ✅ | Old consumers ignore it (tolerant reader) | | Remove an optional field | ⚠️ | Safe only if no consumer depends on it | | Rename a field | ❌ | Add the new field, deprecate the old, remove later | | Change a field's type | ❌ | Introduce a new field or new message version | | Change the meaning of a field | ❌❌ | Silent corruption; always a new message type | **Practices:** - **Tolerant Reader:** consumers ignore unknown fields and use defaults for missing ones. - **Version in the type name** (`OrderPlaced.v2`) or a `schemaVersion` header; run v1 and v2 side by side during migration. - **Schema registry** (Confluent Schema Registry, Apicurio, AWS Glue, Azure Schema Registry) with compatibility modes (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL) enforced at publish time. - **Binary formats** (Avro, Protobuf) give compact payloads and explicit evolution rules; JSON is human-friendly but needs discipline (JSON Schema). - **Consumer-driven contract tests** (Pact supports message contracts). --- ## 4.10 Observability for Messaging | Signal | What to watch | Why | |---|---|---| | **Queue depth / consumer lag** | Messages waiting (RabbitMQ ready count, Kafka lag, SQS `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible`) | Consumers falling behind | | **Age of oldest message** | SQS `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage`, lag in time | User-facing delay; SLA breaches | | **Throughput** | Publish/deliver/ack rates | Capacity planning | | **Processing latency** | Handler duration, end-to-end latency (publish → processed) | Performance regressions | | **Error & retry rates** | Nacks, redeliveries | Failing dependencies, poison messages | | **DLQ size** | Count + growth | Data that needs human attention | | **Unacked messages** | RabbitMQ `messages_unacknowledged` | Stuck consumers, prefetch too high | | **Broker health** | Memory/disk alarms, connection churn, partition under-replication | Imminent outage | **Distributed tracing across async hops:** propagate the W3C `traceparent` header in message headers. OpenTelemetry has semantic conventions for messaging spans (`messaging.system`, `messaging.destination.name`, `messaging.operation`), and producer/consumer spans are linked so a trace follows the message across services. --- ## 4.11 Security - **Transport encryption:** TLS between clients and brokers, and between broker nodes. - **Authentication:** username/password, x.509 client certificates, OAuth 2.0 tokens (RabbitMQ supports OAuth 2), SASL (Kafka: SCRAM, OAUTHBEARER, mTLS), IAM (AWS/GCP), Entra ID / managed identities (Azure). - **Authorization:** least privilege per queue/topic — producers write only, consumers read only (RabbitMQ vhost permissions, Kafka ACLs, IAM policies, ASB SAS/RBAC). - **Payload protection:** encrypt sensitive fields (PII, card data) end-to-end; brokers and DLQs are often less protected than databases. - **Multi-tenancy:** RabbitMQ virtual hosts, Kafka ACL prefixes/quotas, separate namespaces/accounts. - **Input validation:** consumers must validate messages like any external input — a malicious or buggy producer can inject bad data. --- ## 4.12 Interview Talking Points | Question | Strong answer | |---|---| | Can a message be lost? Where? | Between producer and broker (no confirms), inside the broker (no persistence/replication), between broker and consumer (auto-ack before processing). Fix with confirms, durable replicated queues and manual acks after processing. | | Can it be processed twice? | Yes, with at-least-once: lost acks, crashes before ack, producer retries. Make consumers idempotent. | | Exactly-once? | Not end-to-end; get effectively-once with at-least-once + idempotency (+ outbox). Kafka EOS covers Kafka-to-Kafka flows only. | | How do you keep order? | Per-key ordering through partition keys/sessions/message groups; avoid global ordering; or design order-independent handlers. | | How do you evolve message schemas? | Additive, backward-compatible changes; tolerant readers; versioned types; schema registry with compatibility checks. | | What would you monitor? | Lag/queue depth, age of oldest message, error/retry rate, DLQ size, end-to-end latency, broker health, with traces across hops. |
keyConcepts: exactly-once processing limits (Kafka EOS, SQS FIFO)

title: Message Broker Landscape — Kinds and Products
bodyMd:
# 5. Message Broker Landscape — Kinds and Products ## Table of Contents - [5.1 Families of Messaging Technology](#51-families-of-messaging-technology) - [5.2 Queue-Based vs Log-Based: The Core Split](#52-queue-based-vs-log-based-the-core-split) - [5.3 Protocols](#53-protocols) - [5.4 Product Profiles](#54-product-profiles) - [5.5 Big Comparison Table](#55-big-comparison-table) - [5.6 Cloud Equivalents](#56-cloud-equivalents) - [5.7 How to Choose](#57-how-to-choose) - [5.8 Interview Talking Points](#58-interview-talking-points) --- > **Purpose:** Know the major messaging products well enough to compare them, justify a choice in a system design interview, and avoid classic mismatches (e.g. using Kafka as a job queue, or RabbitMQ as an event store). --- ## 5.1 Families of Messaging Technology ```mermaid mindmap root((Messaging Tech)) Traditional brokers RabbitMQ ActiveMQ Classic / Artemis IBM MQ Azure Service Bus Amazon SQS / SNS / MQ Event streaming logs Apache Kafka Apache Pulsar Redpanda Amazon Kinesis Azure Event Hubs Redis Streams Lightweight pub/sub NATS / JetStream Redis Pub/Sub MQTT brokers Event routers AWS EventBridge Azure Event Grid Google Eventarc Brokerless libraries ZeroMQ nanomsg / NNG Task queues Celery Sidekiq BullMQ Hangfire ``` | Family | Core idea | Sweet spot | |---|---|---| | **Traditional message brokers** | Smart broker: routing, per-message acks, deletes after consumption | Commands, work queues, complex routing, enterprise integration | | **Event streaming platforms (logs)** | Append-only partitioned log; consumers track offsets; retention & replay | High-throughput event pipelines, event sourcing feeds, analytics, CDC | | **Lightweight pub/sub** | Minimal overhead, often in-memory | Real-time signals, IoT, service-to-service notifications | | **Event routers (serverless)** | Rule-based filtering and push delivery to targets | SaaS/cloud event integration, serverless workflows | | **Brokerless libraries** | Messaging patterns over sockets, no server | Ultra-low latency, embedded, HPC | | **Task/job queues** | Library on top of Redis/RabbitMQ/DB for background jobs | Background jobs inside one application stack | --- ## 5.2 Queue-Based vs Log-Based: The Core Split ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph QB["Queue-based (RabbitMQ, SQS, ASB)"] direction LR QP[Producer] --> QQ[(Queue: m1 m2 m3)] QQ -->|m1| QC1[Consumer 1] QQ -->|m2| QC2[Consumer 2] QN[["m1 deleted after ack"]] end subgraph LB["Log-based (Kafka, Pulsar, Kinesis)"] direction LR LP[Producer] --> LL[(Log: 0 1 2 3 4 5 →)] LL -->|offset 5| G1[Group A: billing] LL -->|offset 2| G2[Group B: analytics] LN[["records retained by time/size,
each group has its own offset"]] end ``` | Aspect | Queue-based broker | Log-based streaming | |---|---|---| | Message lifetime | Deleted once acked | Retained for a period (or forever / compacted) | | Consumer state | Tracked by the broker per message | Tracked by the consumer as an offset per partition | | Replay | Not possible (once consumed, gone) — except RabbitMQ Streams | Rewind offsets and reprocess any time | | Ordering | Per queue, broken by competing consumers | Strict per partition | | Parallelism | Add consumers freely | Bounded by the number of partitions per group | | Routing | Rich (exchanges, filters, headers) | Simple (topic + key); filtering done by consumers | | Per-message features | TTL, priority, delay, per-message DLQ | Limited; retries/DLQ built by the application | | Throughput | Tens of thousands of msgs/s per node (more with streams) | Millions of msgs/s per cluster | | Best for | Commands, task distribution, RPC, complex routing | Event streams, analytics, event-driven data integration, replay | > **Memorable phrasing:** *RabbitMQ is a post office (deliver and forget); Kafka is a newspaper archive (publish once, anyone can read any issue, any time).* --- ## 5.3 Protocols | Protocol | Description | Supported by | |---|---|---| | **AMQP 0-9-1** | Binary protocol with exchanges, queues, bindings | RabbitMQ (native), LavinMQ | | **AMQP 1.0** | OASIS standard, different model (links, nodes) | Azure Service Bus, ActiveMQ Artemis, Solace, RabbitMQ 4.x (native) | | **MQTT** | Lightweight pub/sub for IoT; QoS 0/1/2, retained messages, last will | Mosquitto, EMQX, HiveMQ, RabbitMQ plugin, AWS IoT Core, Azure Event Grid | | **STOMP** | Simple text protocol, good for browsers/websockets | ActiveMQ, RabbitMQ plugin | | **Kafka protocol** | Binary protocol of Kafka, now a de facto standard | Kafka, Redpanda, Azure Event Hubs, Amazon MSK, WarpStream, Confluent | | **JMS** | A Java **API**, not a wire protocol | ActiveMQ, IBM MQ, Artemis | | **HTTP/webhooks** | Push/pull over HTTP | Cloud services, EventBridge, Event Grid, Pub/Sub push | | **NATS protocol** | Simple text protocol | NATS | | **CloudEvents** | Standard **event envelope** format (not a transport), CNCF | EventBridge (via mapping), Event Grid, Eventarc, Knative, Kafka bindings | --- ## 5.4 Product Profiles ### RabbitMQ - **Type:** Traditional broker (Erlang), AMQP 0-9-1 native, AMQP 1.0 native since 4.0, MQTT/STOMP via plugins. - **Model:** Producers publish to **exchanges** (direct, fanout, topic, headers); **bindings** route to **queues** (classic, **quorum** — Raft-replicated, **streams** — append-only logs with replay). - **Strengths:** flexible routing, per-message acks, DLX, TTL, priorities, mature tooling, great .NET/Java/Python/Node clients, easy to run. - **Weaknesses:** not designed for long retention/replay at massive scale (streams help); clustering needs care. - **Use for:** microservice commands/events, work queues, RPC, complex routing. - → See the dedicated deep-dive file. ### Apache Kafka - **Type:** Distributed event streaming platform (JVM). KRaft mode replaces ZooKeeper (ZooKeeper removed in Kafka 4.0). - **Model:** Topics split into **partitions** (ordered logs), replicated across brokers; **consumer groups** share partitions; offsets committed by consumers. - **Strengths:** huge throughput, durable retention, replay, log compaction, ecosystem (Kafka Connect, Kafka Streams, ksqlDB, Schema Registry, Flink integration). - **Weaknesses:** operational complexity, no per-message routing/priorities/delays, retries and DLQs are DIY, parallelism capped by partitions (share groups / "queues for Kafka", KIP-932, are arriving to address queue use cases). - **Use for:** event backbones, CDC, stream processing, analytics pipelines, event sourcing feeds. - → See the dedicated deep-dive file. ### ActiveMQ (Classic and Artemis) - **Type:** Java broker, JMS 1.1/2.0 (Artemis also Jakarta Messaging 3.x), multi-protocol (OpenWire, AMQP 1.0, STOMP, MQTT). - **Strengths:** JMS ecosystem, XA transactions, multi-protocol; Artemis is the high-performance next generation (and the base of Red Hat AMQ Broker), while Amazon MQ offers managed ActiveMQ Classic. - **Use for:** Java enterprise integration, JMS-based legacy systems. ### IBM MQ - **Type:** Enterprise broker with decades of use in banking/mainframes. - **Strengths:** rock-solid transactional delivery, mainframe integration, exactly-once with XA. - **Use for:** regulated industries and existing IBM estates. ### Amazon SQS & SNS - **SQS:** fully managed queues. **Standard** (nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once, best-effort ordering) and **FIFO** (ordered per `MessageGroupId`, dedup within 5 min). Visibility timeout, long polling (≤20 s), DLQ via redrive policy, retention 1 min–14 days (default 4 days), delay up to 15 min. - **SNS:** managed pub/sub topics; fans out to SQS, Lambda, HTTP, email, SMS; message filtering policies. **SNS → SQS fan-out** is the classic AWS pub/sub pattern. - **Use for:** AWS-native decoupling with zero ops. ### Amazon MQ Managed **RabbitMQ** or **ActiveMQ** — lift-and-shift of existing broker workloads to AWS. ### Azure Service Bus - **Type:** Managed enterprise broker (AMQP 1.0). - **Features:** queues, **topics with subscriptions** and SQL/correlation filters, **sessions** (FIFO per session ID, stateful), dead-letter sub-queues, duplicate detection, scheduled messages, deferral, transactions across entities, peek-lock and receive-and-delete modes, auto-forwarding. - **Tiers:** Basic (queues only), Standard (topics), Premium (dedicated resources, large messages up to 100 MB, geo-DR, VNet). - **Use for:** Azure microservices, enterprise workflows needing ordering and transactions. ### Azure Event Hubs Managed event streaming (log-based), **Kafka protocol compatible**, partitions + consumer groups, Capture to storage. The Azure equivalent of Kafka/Kinesis. ### Google Cloud Pub/Sub - Global managed pub/sub: topics + subscriptions (pull, push, BigQuery/Cloud Storage export). - Ack deadlines, ordering keys, exactly-once delivery (pull), dead-letter topics, retention and **seek/replay** (to a timestamp or snapshot). - **Use for:** GCP-native messaging and ingestion; sits between a queue and a log. ### Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Managed log-based streaming with **shards** (similar to partitions), retention 24 h up to 365 days. AWS-native alternative to Kafka (Amazon MSK is managed Kafka). ### Apache Pulsar - **Type:** Streaming + queuing in one; compute (brokers) separated from storage (**Apache BookKeeper**), tiered storage to object stores. - **Subscriptions:** exclusive, failover, **shared** (queue semantics) and **key_shared** (ordered per key with parallelism). - **Strengths:** multi-tenancy, geo-replication built in, both queue and stream semantics. - **Weaknesses:** more moving parts (brokers + bookies + metadata store), smaller ecosystem than Kafka. ### Redpanda Kafka-API-compatible streaming engine written in C++ (no JVM, no ZooKeeper), single binary, lower tail latency. Drop-in for Kafka clients. ### NATS & JetStream - **NATS Core:** extremely fast, simple **subject-based** pub/sub (`orders.*.created`, `orders.>` wildcards), at-most-once, request-reply built in, queue groups for load balancing. - **JetStream:** persistence layer — streams, consumers (push/pull), at-least-once, dedup by message ID, key-value and object stores. - **Use for:** cloud-native microservices, edge/IoT, low-latency service mesh-style messaging. ### Redis Pub/Sub and Redis Streams - **Pub/Sub:** fire-and-forget broadcast, no persistence — offline subscribers miss messages. - **Streams:** append-only log with **consumer groups** (`XADD`, `XREADGROUP`, `XACK`, pending entries list, `XCLAIM`/`XAUTOCLAIM` for stuck messages). - **Use for:** lightweight queues/streams when Redis is already in the stack; not a replacement for a durable broker at scale (memory-bound). ### MQTT brokers (Mosquitto, EMQX, HiveMQ, VerneMQ) Pub/sub for constrained devices: tiny headers, QoS 0/1/2, retained messages, last-will messages, persistent sessions. Often bridged into Kafka or a cloud pipeline. ### ZeroMQ A messaging **library**, not a broker: socket patterns (REQ/REP, PUB/SUB, PUSH/PULL, ROUTER/DEALER) with in-memory queues. No persistence; you build the topology. Used in trading systems, scientific computing, Jupyter kernels. ### Task queues (Celery, Sidekiq, BullMQ, Hangfire, RQ) Libraries for **background jobs** within an application ecosystem, using Redis/RabbitMQ/SQL as the backing store. They add job semantics: retries, scheduling, priorities, rate limiting, dashboards. Great for "run this function later"; not for cross-team integration contracts. --- ## 5.5 Big Comparison Table | Product | Model | Delivery | Ordering | Replay | Routing | Throughput | Ops burden | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | **RabbitMQ** | Queue broker (+ streams) | At-most / at-least once | Per queue (single consumer) | Streams only | ★★★★★ exchanges | High | Medium | | **Kafka** | Partitioned log | At-least once; EOS within Kafka | Per partition | ✅ | ★★ topic + key | ★★★★★ | High (lower with managed) | | **Pulsar** | Segmented log + queues | At-least once; EOS (transactions) | Per partition / key_shared | ✅ | ★★★ | ★★★★★ | High | | **ActiveMQ Artemis** | Queue broker (JMS) | At-least once; XA | Per queue / message groups | ❌ | ★★★★ | High | Medium | | **NATS JetStream** | Subject pub/sub + streams | At-most (core) / at-least (JS) | Per stream | ✅ | ★★★★ subjects | ★★★★ | Low | | **Redis Streams** | In-memory log | At-least once | Per stream | ✅ (memory-bound) | ★ | ★★★★ | Low (if Redis exists) | | **Amazon SQS** | Managed queue | At-least once (Standard), dedup (FIFO) | FIFO per group | ❌ | ★ | ★★★★★ (Standard) | None | | **Amazon SNS** | Managed pub/sub | At-least once | FIFO topics | ❌ | ★★★ filter policies | ★★★★★ | None | | **Azure Service Bus** | Managed broker | At-least once; dedup; transactions | Sessions | ❌ | ★★★★ SQL filters | High | None | | **Google Pub/Sub** | Managed pub/sub | At-least / exactly-once (pull) | Ordering keys | Seek/snapshot | ★★★ filters | ★★★★★ | None | | **Kinesis / Event Hubs** | Managed log | At-least once | Per shard/partition | ✅ | ★ | ★★★★★ | Low | | **ZeroMQ** | Library | At-most once | Per socket | ❌ | Patterns | ★★★★★ latency | You build it | --- ## 5.6 Cloud Equivalents | Capability | AWS | Azure | Google Cloud | Open source | |---|---|---|---|---| | Queue | SQS | Service Bus queues / Storage Queues | Pub/Sub (pull) / Cloud Tasks | RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ | | Pub/sub topic | SNS | Service Bus topics | Pub/Sub | RabbitMQ exchanges, NATS | | Event streaming log | Kinesis, MSK (Kafka) | Event Hubs | Pub/Sub, Managed Kafka | Kafka, Pulsar, Redpanda | | Event router / event bus | EventBridge | Event Grid | Eventarc | Knative Eventing, Argo Events | | Managed traditional broker | Amazon MQ | — (Service Bus) | — | — | | Workflow orchestration | Step Functions | Durable Functions, Logic Apps | Workflows | Temporal, Camunda | --- ## 5.7 How to Choose ```mermaid flowchart TD S[What do you need?] --> R{Replay history /
multiple independent readers
at their own pace?} R -- Yes --> T{Throughput &
ecosystem needs} T -- Massive, stream processing --> K[Kafka / Redpanda /
Event Hubs / Kinesis] T -- Multi-tenant, geo, queue + stream --> PU[Pulsar] R -- No --> W{Mainly commands,
jobs, complex routing?} W -- Yes --> C{Run it yourself
or managed?} C -- Self-hosted --> RMQ[RabbitMQ] C -- Managed AWS --> SQS[SQS + SNS] C -- Managed Azure --> ASB[Azure Service Bus] C -- Managed GCP --> PS[Google Pub/Sub] W -- No --> L{Ultra-low latency,
loss acceptable?} L -- Yes --> N[NATS Core / Redis Pub/Sub / ZeroMQ] L -- No --> E{Routing cloud & SaaS events
to serverless targets?} E -- Yes --> EB[EventBridge / Event Grid / Eventarc] E -- No --> J[Background jobs in one app:
Celery, BullMQ, Hangfire, Sidekiq] ``` **Questions to ask before choosing:** 1. Commands/jobs or events/streams? Do consumers need **replay**? 2. Required **throughput** and **latency**? Message **size**? 3. **Ordering** requirements: none, per key, global? 4. **Delivery guarantee** needed? Tolerance for duplicates/loss? 5. **Routing complexity**: simple fan-out or content-based routing? 6. **Retention**: minutes, days, forever? 7. **Operational capacity**: can the team run a cluster, or must it be managed? 8. **Cloud / vendor** constraints, **cost** model, **compliance** (data residency, encryption)? 9. **Ecosystem**: connectors, stream processing, client libraries for your languages? --- ## 5.8 Interview Talking Points | Question | Strong answer | |---|---| | RabbitMQ vs Kafka? | RabbitMQ is a smart broker that routes and deletes messages after ack — ideal for commands, work queues and routing. Kafka is a distributed log that retains events for replay with per-partition ordering and massive throughput — ideal for event streams and data pipelines. | | SQS vs SNS? | SQS is a queue (pull, one consumer per message); SNS is a pub/sub topic (push to many). Combine them for fan-out with durable per-service queues. | | Why not Redis as a broker? | Pub/Sub loses messages for offline subscribers; Streams are memory-bound with fewer guarantees and tooling than dedicated brokers — fine for lightweight use. | | When Pulsar over Kafka? | When you need native multi-tenancy, geo-replication, tiered storage and both queue (shared subscriptions) and stream semantics in one system. | | What's CloudEvents? | A CNCF specification for a common event envelope (id, source, type, time, data…), so events are portable across brokers and clouds. |
keyConcepts: messaging protocols: AMQP, MQTT, STOMP, Kafka protocol
RabbitMQ, Kafka, ActiveMQ, Pulsar, NATS, Redis Streams
Amazon SQS/SNS, Azure Service Bus, Google Pub/Sub

title: RabbitMQ Deep Dive
bodyMd:
# 6. RabbitMQ Deep Dive ## Table of Contents - [6.1 What RabbitMQ Is](#61-what-rabbitmq-is) - [6.2 The AMQP 0-9-1 Model](#62-the-amqp-0-9-1-model) - [6.3 Exchange Types](#63-exchange-types) - [6.4 Queue Types: Classic, Quorum, Streams](#64-queue-types-classic-quorum-streams) - [6.5 Connections, Channels and Consumers](#65-connections-channels-and-consumers) - [6.6 Reliability: Confirms, Acks, Persistence](#66-reliability-confirms-acks-persistence) - [6.7 Dead Lettering, TTL, Retries and Delays](#67-dead-lettering-ttl-retries-and-delays) - [6.8 Prefetch, Flow Control and Performance](#68-prefetch-flow-control-and-performance) - [6.9 Clustering, High Availability and Federation](#69-clustering-high-availability-and-federation) - [6.10 Code Examples](#610-code-examples) - [6.11 Typical Topologies for Microservices](#611-typical-topologies-for-microservices) - [6.12 Operations and Monitoring](#612-operations-and-monitoring) - [6.13 Anti-Patterns](#613-anti-patterns) - [6.14 Interview Talking Points](#614-interview-talking-points) --- > **Purpose:** RabbitMQ is the most widely deployed open-source message broker and the default "message bus transport" for many microservice stacks (especially .NET with MassTransit/NServiceBus, Spring AMQP, Celery). Know its model cold. --- ## 6.1 What RabbitMQ Is - Open-source message broker written in **Erlang/OTP** (now maintained by Broadcom / VMware Tanzu team). - Speaks **AMQP 0-9-1** natively; **AMQP 1.0** natively since **RabbitMQ 4.0**; **MQTT** and **STOMP** (also over WebSockets) via plugins; has a **Stream protocol** for streams. - Ports: **5672** (AMQP), **5671** (AMQPS), **15672** (management UI/HTTP API), **5552** (streams), **1883** (MQTT), **61613** (STOMP). - Key 4.x changes: classic queue **mirroring removed** (use quorum queues), **Khepri** (Raft-based) metadata store replacing Mnesia, quorum queues default delivery-limit of 20. --- ## 6.2 The AMQP 0-9-1 Model **Producers never publish directly to queues.** They publish to an **exchange** with a **routing key**; the exchange routes copies to **queues** according to **bindings**; consumers read from queues. ```mermaid flowchart LR P[Producer] -->|"publish(exchange='orders',
routingKey='order.created.eu')"| X{{Exchange: orders
type: topic}} X -->|"binding: order.created.*"| Q1[(queue: billing)] X -->|"binding: order.#"| Q2[(queue: audit)] X -->|"binding: *.*.us"| Q3[(queue: us-warehouse)] Q1 --> C1[Billing consumer] Q2 --> C2[Audit consumer] style X fill:#EF5350,color:#fff ``` | Concept | Description | |---|---| | **Virtual host (vhost)** | Logical namespace with its own exchanges, queues and permissions — multi-tenancy | | **Exchange** | Routing agent; has a name, type, durability | | **Binding** | Rule linking an exchange to a queue (or another exchange) with a binding key / arguments | | **Routing key** | String attached to each message, matched against bindings | | **Queue** | Ordered buffer storing messages until consumed; durable/transient, exclusive, auto-delete | | **Message** | Body (bytes) + properties (`delivery_mode`, `content_type`, `message_id`, `correlation_id`, `reply_to`, `expiration`, `priority`, `headers`) | | **Default exchange** (`""`) | Pre-declared direct exchange; every queue is bound to it with its own name → "publish to a queue by name" | --- ## 6.3 Exchange Types | Type | Routing rule | Typical use | |---|---|---| | **Direct** | Routing key **equals** binding key | Commands to a specific queue, routing by severity/type | | **Fanout** | Ignores routing key, copies to **all** bound queues | Broadcast events | | **Topic** | Pattern match on dot-separated words: `*` = exactly one word, `#` = zero or more words | Event routing by category/region | | **Headers** | Matches message headers (`x-match: all` or `any`) instead of routing key | Routing on multiple attributes | | **Consistent hash** (plugin) | Hashes the routing key to distribute across queues | Partitioned, per-key ordered processing | | **Delayed message** (plugin) | Holds messages until `x-delay` elapses | Scheduled delivery | | **Exchange-to-exchange bindings** | Exchanges bound to exchanges | Layered routing topologies | ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Direct PD[Producer] -->|rk=error| XD{{direct}} XD -->|bk=error| QE[(errors)] XD -.->|bk=info| QI[(info)] end subgraph Fanout PF[Producer] --> XF{{fanout}} XF --> QF1[(q1)] XF --> QF2[(q2)] XF --> QF3[(q3)] end subgraph Topic PT[Producer] -->|rk=stock.nyse.ibm| XT{{topic}} XT -->|stock.nyse.*| QT1[(nyse)] XT -->|stock.#| QT2[(all stocks)] XT -.->|stock.nasdaq.*| QT3[(nasdaq)] end ``` **Topic matching examples** for routing key `order.created.eu`: | Binding key | Match? | |---|---| | `order.created.eu` | ✅ | | `order.*.eu` | ✅ | | `order.#` | ✅ | | `#` | ✅ (everything) | | `order.*` | ❌ (`*` is exactly one word) | | `*.created` | ❌ | **Alternate exchange:** messages that match no binding are normally dropped (or returned with `mandatory`). An `alternate-exchange` argument sends them to a catch-all exchange instead. --- ## 6.4 Queue Types: Classic, Quorum, Streams | Feature | Classic queue | Quorum queue | Stream | |---|---|---|---| | Replication | None (single node) in 4.x | **Raft** across nodes (typically 3 or 5) | Replicated log | | Data safety | Lost if the node's disk is lost | Survives minority node failures | Survives minority failures | | Consumption | Destructive (deleted on ack) | Destructive | **Non-destructive** — read from any offset, replay | | Poison message handling | Manual | **Delivery limit** (default 20 in 4.x) → DLX | N/A | | Priorities | ✅ (`x-max-priority`) | ✅ (simplified, 4.0+) | ❌ | | Non-durable / exclusive | ✅ | ❌ (always durable) | ❌ | | Use for | Temporary/exclusive queues, reply queues, non-critical data | **Default for durable business queues** | Large fan-out, replay, very long queues, high throughput | ```bash # Declare a quorum queue with the management CLI rabbitmqadmin declare queue name=billing durable=true arguments='{"x-queue-type":"quorum"}' ``` > **Super streams** partition a stream across several streams (like Kafka partitions) for scaling with per-key ordering. --- ## 6.5 Connections, Channels and Consumers ```mermaid flowchart LR APP[Application process] -->|one long-lived TCP connection| BR[RabbitMQ node] subgraph Conn["Connection (TCP, TLS, auth)"] CH1[Channel 1: publishing] CH2[Channel 2: consumer A] CH3[Channel 3: consumer B] end APP --- Conn ``` - **Connection:** expensive TCP (+TLS) connection — keep **long-lived**, typically one or two per process (separate for publishing and consuming so publisher flow control doesn't block consumers). - **Channel:** lightweight virtual connection multiplexed over a connection. **Not thread-safe** in most clients — use one per thread/consumer. - **Consumer:** subscription on a channel (`basic.consume`); the broker pushes messages. `basic.get` (polling) exists but is inefficient. - **Exclusive consumer / single active consumer:** only one consumer receives messages at a time; others are on standby — preserves order with failover. --- ## 6.6 Reliability: Confirms, Acks, Persistence To avoid message loss you need **all four**: | Layer | Setting | |---|---| | Queue survives restart | `durable=true` (quorum queues are always durable) | | Message survives restart | `delivery_mode=2` (persistent) | | Producer knows it was stored | **Publisher confirms** (`confirm.select`), handle `basic.ack`/`basic.nack` from broker | | Consumer doesn't lose on crash | **Manual acks** (`autoAck=false`), ack after processing | Additional safeguards: - `mandatory=true` + return handler (or alternate exchange) to detect **unroutable** messages. - **Quorum queues** for replication. - **Consumer acknowledgement timeout** (`consumer_timeout`, default 30 minutes) closes channels that never ack — protects against stuck consumers. Consumer responses: | Method | Effect | |---|---| | `basic.ack` | Processed — delete | | `basic.nack(requeue=true)` | Put back in the queue (careful: immediate tight loops) | | `basic.nack(requeue=false)` / `basic.reject` | Discard or **dead-letter** if a DLX is configured | | `multiple=true` | Ack/nack all deliveries up to this tag (batching) | --- ## 6.7 Dead Lettering, TTL, Retries and Delays A message is **dead-lettered** when it is rejected with `requeue=false`, its **TTL expires**, the queue exceeds its **length limit**, or a quorum queue's **delivery limit** is exceeded. ```mermaid flowchart LR P[Producer] --> X{{orders}} X --> Q[(billing
x-dead-letter-exchange: billing.dlx)] Q --> C[Consumer] C -->|reject requeue=false| Q Q -->|dead-letter| DLX{{billing.dlx}} DLX --> DLQ[(billing.dlq)] style DLQ fill:#757575,color:#fff ``` ### Delayed retry with TTL + DLX ("retry queue" pattern) ```mermaid flowchart LR Q[(work)] -->|reject| DLX1{{work.retry}} DLX1 --> RQ[(work.retry.30s
x-message-ttl: 30000
x-dead-letter-exchange: work)] RQ -->|TTL expires → dead-letter| W{{work exchange}} W --> Q ``` - Failed messages go to a **wait queue** without consumers; when the TTL expires they are dead-lettered **back** to the work exchange. - Use several wait queues (10 s, 1 min, 10 min) for exponential backoff, and count attempts with the `x-death` header (or a custom header); after N attempts route to a final DLQ. - Alternative: the **delayed message exchange plugin** (`x-delayed-type`, `x-delay` header) — simpler, but delayed messages are stored on a single node (not replicated). - Bus frameworks (MassTransit, NServiceBus) implement delayed redelivery for you. ### Queue arguments cheat sheet | Argument | Purpose | |---|---| | `x-queue-type` | `classic`, `quorum`, `stream` | | `x-dead-letter-exchange` / `x-dead-letter-routing-key` | Where dead letters go | | `x-message-ttl` | Per-queue message TTL (ms) | | `x-expires` | Delete the queue after inactivity | | `x-max-length` / `x-max-length-bytes` | Bound the queue | | `x-overflow` | `drop-head` (default), `reject-publish`, `reject-publish-dlx` | | `x-max-priority` | Enable priorities | | `x-delivery-limit` | Quorum queue poison message limit | | `x-single-active-consumer` | Only one consumer active at a time | > Prefer **policies** (`rabbitmqctl set_policy`) over hard-coded queue arguments where possible: policies can be changed at runtime without redeclaring queues. --- ## 6.8 Prefetch, Flow Control and Performance **Prefetch (`basic.qos`)** = maximum unacked messages delivered to a consumer. | Prefetch | Effect | |---|---| | Unlimited (0) | Broker floods one consumer; memory pressure; poor load balancing | | 1 | Perfectly fair dispatch but low throughput (round-trip per message) | | 10–300 | Typical sweet spot; tune with measurement | **Flow control & alarms:** - **Memory high watermark** (default 0.6 of RAM) and **disk free limit** trigger **alarms** that **block publishers** cluster-wide until resolved. - Credit-based flow control slows fast publishers per connection. **Performance tips:** - Keep queues **short** — RabbitMQ is happiest when messages flow through quickly; very long queues hurt (use streams if you need backlog/retention). - Use **multiple queues** to spread load across cores/nodes (a single queue is bound to one Erlang process/leader). - Batch publisher confirms (async confirms) instead of waiting for each one. - Reuse connections and channels; avoid opening a connection per message. - Messages ideally small (KBs); use Claim Check for large payloads. --- ## 6.9 Clustering, High Availability and Federation | Mechanism | Purpose | Notes | |---|---|---| | **Cluster** | Several nodes sharing metadata (users, vhosts, exchanges, queues) in one LAN/region | Use an **odd number** of nodes (3, 5) for quorum | | **Quorum queues / streams** | Data replication & failover | Leader + followers via Raft | | **Federation plugin** | Loosely link brokers across WAN/regions; exchanges/queues receive messages from upstreams | Tolerant to latency and partitions | | **Shovel plugin** | Move messages from a source to a destination (queue → exchange) across brokers | Migrations, bridging | | **Warm standby / schema sync** | Commercial (Tanzu RabbitMQ) cross-cluster replication | DR | **Network partitions:** with quorum queues, the minority side cannot accept writes for those queues (CP behavior). Plan cluster placement across availability zones with low latency. **Running on Kubernetes:** use the **RabbitMQ Cluster Kubernetes Operator** and the **Messaging Topology Operator** (declare exchanges/queues/bindings as CRDs). --- ## 6.10 Code Examples ### Node.js (amqplib) — topic exchange with DLX ```typescript import amqp from 'amqplib'; const conn = await amqp.connect('amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672'); // ── Topology ─────────────────────────────────────────── const setup = await conn.createChannel(); await setup.assertExchange('orders', 'topic', { durable: true }); await setup.assertExchange('billing.dlx', 'fanout', { durable: true }); await setup.assertQueue('billing.dlq', { durable: true, arguments: { 'x-queue-type': 'quorum' } }); await setup.bindQueue('billing.dlq', 'billing.dlx', ''); await setup.assertQueue('billing', { durable: true, arguments: { 'x-queue-type': 'quorum', 'x-dead-letter-exchange': 'billing.dlx', 'x-delivery-limit': 5, }, }); await setup.bindQueue('billing', 'orders', 'order.created.*'); // ── Publisher with confirms ──────────────────────────── const pub = await conn.createConfirmChannel(); pub.publish('orders', 'order.created.eu', Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ orderId: '42', total: 99.5 })), { persistent: true, contentType: 'application/json', messageId: crypto.randomUUID() }); await pub.waitForConfirms(); // ── Consumer with manual ack ─────────────────────────── const sub = await conn.createChannel(); await sub.prefetch(50); await sub.consume('billing', async msg => { if (!msg) return; try { const order = JSON.parse(msg.content.toString()); await createInvoice(order); // idempotent sub.ack(msg); } catch (err) { sub.nack(msg, false, false); // dead-letter (no requeue) } }, { noAck: false }); ``` ### C# (RabbitMQ.Client 7.x, async API) ```csharp var factory = new ConnectionFactory { HostName = "localhost" }; await using var connection = await factory.CreateConnectionAsync(); // Publisher confirms are enabled through channel options in 7.x await using var channel = await connection.CreateChannelAsync( new CreateChannelOptions(publisherConfirmationsEnabled: true, publisherConfirmationTrackingEnabled: true)); await channel.ExchangeDeclareAsync("orders", ExchangeType.Topic, durable: true); var body = JsonSerializer.SerializeToUtf8Bytes(new { OrderId = 42, Total = 99.5m }); var props = new BasicProperties { Persistent = true, ContentType = "application/json", MessageId = Guid.NewGuid().ToString() }; // Awaiting completes when the broker confirms (throws on nack/return) await channel.BasicPublishAsync("orders", "order.created.eu", mandatory: true, props, body); ``` ### Python — RPC with Direct Reply-To ```python import pika, uuid conn = pika.BlockingConnection(pika.ConnectionParameters("localhost")) ch = conn.channel() corr_id = str(uuid.uuid4()) response = None def on_reply(ch, method, props, body): global response if props.correlation_id == corr_id: response = body # Pseudo-queue: no need to declare a reply queue ch.basic_consume(queue="amq.rabbitmq.reply-to", on_message_callback=on_reply, auto_ack=True) ch.basic_publish(exchange="", routing_key="pricing.rpc", properties=pika.BasicProperties(reply_to="amq.rabbitmq.reply-to", correlation_id=corr_id), body=b'{"sku":"ABC"}') while response is None: conn.process_data_events(time_limit=1) ``` --- ## 6.11 Typical Topologies for Microservices ### Events: one exchange per event type, one queue per subscribing service ```mermaid flowchart LR OS[Order Service] -->|publish| X1{{"exchange: OrderPlaced (fanout)"}} X1 --> QB[(billing.order-placed)] X1 --> QI[(inventory.order-placed)] X1 --> QN[(notifications.order-placed)] QB --> B1[billing #1] QB --> B2[billing #2] QI --> I1[inventory] QN --> N1[notifications] ``` This is exactly what **MassTransit** creates by convention (exchange per message type, exchange-to-exchange bindings, queue per endpoint). ### Commands: queue per receiving endpoint ```mermaid flowchart LR API[Checkout API] -->|send ChargeCustomer| QP[(payments)] ADM[Admin UI] -->|send ChargeCustomer| QP QP --> P1[payments #1] QP --> P2[payments #2] ``` ### Topic exchange for region/category routing Routing keys like `..` (`order.created.eu`) and bindings per need: `order.*.eu`, `order.cancelled.*`, `#`. --- ## 6.12 Operations and Monitoring | Tool | Use | |---|---| | **Management UI** (`:15672`) | Inspect queues, rates, connections; publish/get test messages | | **rabbitmqctl / rabbitmq-diagnostics / rabbitmq-queues** | Cluster status, health checks, policies, quorum membership | | **Prometheus plugin** (`rabbitmq_prometheus`, port 15692) + Grafana dashboards | Production metrics | | **Definitions export/import** | Version-control topology (users, vhosts, exchanges, queues, bindings, policies) | Key metrics: `messages_ready`, `messages_unacknowledged`, publish/deliver/ack rates, consumer count per queue (0 = trouble), memory/disk alarms, file descriptors, connection churn, quorum queue leader distribution, DLQ depth. --- ## 6.13 Anti-Patterns | Anti-pattern | Why it hurts | Fix | |---|---|---| | Opening a connection per message | Huge overhead, connection churn | Long-lived connections, pooled channels | | Sharing a channel across threads | Frame interleaving errors | One channel per thread | | `autoAck=true` for business messages | Loss on consumer crash | Manual acks after processing | | `nack(requeue=true)` on every error | Tight infinite loop, CPU burn | Delayed retry + delivery limit + DLQ | | Unlimited prefetch | One consumer hoards messages, memory blow-up | Set prefetch | | Using RabbitMQ as a database / long-term store | Long queues degrade performance | Keep queues short; use streams or a DB | | Classic non-replicated queues for critical data | Data loss on node failure | Quorum queues | | Huge messages (MBs) | Memory pressure, slow replication | Claim Check | | Declaring topology ad hoc in every service without conventions | Drift, unexpected bindings | Conventions (bus framework), definitions, operators | --- ## 6.14 Interview Talking Points | Question | Strong answer | |---|---| | Explain the RabbitMQ model | Producers publish to exchanges with a routing key; bindings route copies to queues; consumers read from queues and ack. Exchange types: direct, fanout, topic, headers. | | How do you guarantee no message loss? | Durable (quorum) queues, persistent messages, publisher confirms, manual consumer acks after processing, plus mandatory/alternate exchange for unroutable messages. | | Classic vs quorum vs stream? | Classic = single node, fast, for transient queues; quorum = Raft-replicated, durable default with delivery limits; stream = replayable append-only log for fan-out and retention. | | How do you implement retries with backoff? | DLX + TTL wait queues that dead-letter back to the work exchange, the delayed-message plugin, or let the bus framework do delayed redelivery; cap attempts and route to a DLQ. | | How do you preserve ordering? | One queue with a single active consumer, or partition by key with the consistent-hash exchange / super streams; avoid requeue-based retries which reorder. | | How does RabbitMQ handle backpressure? | Credit-based flow control per connection, memory/disk alarms that block publishers, queue length limits with `reject-publish`, and consumer prefetch. |
keyConcepts: direct, fanout, topic and headers exchanges
classic vs quorum queues vs streams
dead-letter exchanges, TTL and delayed retries

title: Apache Kafka & Event Streaming
bodyMd:
# 7. Apache Kafka & Event Streaming ## Table of Contents - [7.1 What Event Streaming Is](#71-what-event-streaming-is) - [7.2 Kafka Architecture](#72-kafka-architecture) - [7.3 Topics, Partitions, Offsets](#73-topics-partitions-offsets) - [7.4 Producers](#74-producers) - [7.5 Consumers and Consumer Groups](#75-consumers-and-consumer-groups) - [7.6 Replication and Durability](#76-replication-and-durability) - [7.7 Retention and Log Compaction](#77-retention-and-log-compaction) - [7.8 Exactly-Once Semantics](#78-exactly-once-semantics) - [7.9 Retries and Dead-Letter Topics](#79-retries-and-dead-letter-topics) - [7.10 The Kafka Ecosystem](#710-the-kafka-ecosystem) - [7.11 Kafka as a Message Bus vs Event Bus](#711-kafka-as-a-message-bus-vs-event-bus) - [7.12 Pitfalls](#712-pitfalls) - [7.13 Interview Talking Points](#713-interview-talking-points) --- > **Purpose:** Kafka is the dominant event streaming platform and appears in almost every system design interview involving events, analytics or high throughput. Understand partitions, consumer groups and guarantees — and why Kafka is *not* just "a faster RabbitMQ". --- ## 7.1 What Event Streaming Is Event streaming treats data as an **unbounded, ordered, replayable sequence of events** stored in a durable **log**. Instead of "send a message to someone", the model is "**append a fact to a log**; anyone may read it, now or later, at their own pace". | Messaging (queue) mindset | Streaming (log) mindset | |---|---| | Message is a task to be done | Event is a fact that happened | | Consumed → deleted | Retained → replayable | | Broker tracks what each consumer got | Consumer tracks its own position (offset) | | New consumer sees only new messages | New consumer can read history from the beginning | --- ## 7.2 Kafka Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Producers P1[Order Service] P2[Payment Service] end subgraph Cluster["Kafka Cluster (KRaft)"] C[Controller quorum
metadata via Raft] B1[Broker 1
P0 leader, P1 follower] B2[Broker 2
P1 leader, P2 follower] B3[Broker 3
P2 leader, P0 follower] end subgraph Consumers G1[Group: billing
2 instances] G2[Group: analytics
3 instances] end P1 --> B1 P2 --> B2 B1 --> G1 B2 --> G1 B3 --> G2 B1 --> G2 C -.manages.-> B1 C -.manages.-> B2 C -.manages.-> B3 ``` | Component | Role | |---|---| | **Broker** | Server storing partitions and serving reads/writes | | **Controller (KRaft)** | Manages cluster metadata (topics, partitions, leaders) using Raft. ZooKeeper mode was deprecated and **removed in Kafka 4.0** | | **Topic** | Named stream of records (e.g. `orders`) | | **Partition** | Ordered, append-only log; unit of parallelism, ordering and replication | | **Replica** | Copy of a partition on another broker; one **leader**, N **followers** | | **Producer** | Appends records to partitions | | **Consumer group** | Set of consumers sharing the work of reading a topic | --- ## 7.3 Topics, Partitions, Offsets ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph T["Topic: orders (3 partitions)"] P0["P0: | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | → "] P1["P1: | 0 | 1 | 2 | → "] P2["P2: | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | → "] end ``` - A **record** = key, value, headers, timestamp. - Each record in a partition gets a monotonically increasing **offset**. - **Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition.** - The **key** decides the partition (`hash(key) % partitions` by default) → all events for the same key (e.g. `orderId`) go to the same partition, in order. - No key → records are spread (sticky partitioner batches to one partition at a time). - Partition count can be increased but **not decreased**, and increasing it changes key→partition mapping (breaks per-key ordering for existing keys). Choose it deliberately (based on target throughput / max consumer parallelism). --- ## 7.4 Producers | Setting | Meaning | Recommended for durability | |---|---|---| | `acks` | `0` = no wait, `1` = leader stored, `all` = all in-sync replicas stored | `all` | | `enable.idempotence` | Broker dedups retries per producer session (sequence numbers) | `true` (default since 3.0) | | `retries` / `delivery.timeout.ms` | How long to keep retrying | High retries, bounded by timeout | | `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` | Parallel requests; ≤ 5 keeps ordering with idempotence | ≤ 5 | | `linger.ms` / `batch.size` | Wait to batch records → throughput | e.g. 5–20 ms | | `compression.type` | `lz4`, `zstd`, `snappy`, `gzip` | `lz4` or `zstd` | ```typescript // KafkaJS producer import { Kafka, CompressionTypes } from 'kafkajs'; const kafka = new Kafka({ clientId: 'order-service', brokers: ['kafka:9092'] }); const producer = kafka.producer({ idempotent: true, maxInFlightRequests: 5 }); await producer.connect(); await producer.send({ topic: 'orders', acks: -1, // all in-sync replicas compression: CompressionTypes.GZIP, messages: [{ key: order.id, // same order → same partition → ordered value: JSON.stringify({ type: 'OrderPlaced', ...order }), headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', traceparent }, }], }); ``` --- ## 7.5 Consumers and Consumer Groups ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Topic["orders: 4 partitions"] P0[P0] P1[P1] P2[P2] P3[P3] end subgraph GA["Group billing (2 consumers)"] A1[consumer A1] A2[consumer A2] end subgraph GB["Group analytics (4 consumers)"] B1[B1] B2[B2] B3[B3] B4[B4] end P0 --> A1 P1 --> A1 P2 --> A2 P3 --> A2 P0 --> B1 P1 --> B2 P2 --> B3 P3 --> B4 ``` - Within a group, **each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer** → queue-like load balancing + per-partition ordering. - **Different groups** each get **all** records → pub/sub. - More consumers than partitions → extra consumers sit **idle**. Max parallelism per group = partition count. - **Offsets** are committed to the internal `__consumer_offsets` topic. On restart or rebalance, consumption resumes from the last committed offset. - **Rebalancing** happens when consumers join/leave; the **cooperative sticky** assignor and the new **consumer group protocol (KIP-848, GA in 4.0)** reduce stop-the-world pauses. - `auto.offset.reset`: `earliest` (read from start) or `latest` (only new records) when no committed offset exists. ```python # confluent-kafka consumer with manual commits (at-least-once) from confluent_kafka import Consumer c = Consumer({ "bootstrap.servers": "kafka:9092", "group.id": "billing", "enable.auto.commit": False, "auto.offset.reset": "earliest", "isolation.level": "read_committed", }) c.subscribe(["orders"]) while True: msg = c.poll(1.0) if msg is None or msg.error(): continue handle(msg.key(), msg.value()) # idempotent processing c.commit(message=msg, asynchronous=False) ``` > **Head-of-line blocking:** because a partition is processed in order, one slow or failing record blocks all records behind it in that partition. Plan retries accordingly (see 7.9). **Share groups (KIP-932, "Queues for Kafka")** — introduced as early access in Kafka 4.0 — let multiple consumers read the *same* partition with per-record acknowledgement, giving queue semantics (no ordering) without the partition-count limit. --- ## 7.6 Replication and Durability | Concept | Description | |---|---| | **Replication factor** | Number of copies of each partition (typically 3) | | **ISR (in-sync replicas)** | Replicas caught up with the leader | | **`min.insync.replicas`** | Minimum ISR count required for an `acks=all` write to succeed (typically 2 with RF=3) | | **Leader election** | If the leader fails, a follower from the ISR becomes leader | | **`unclean.leader.election.enable`** | `false` (default): never elect an out-of-sync replica → no data loss, possible unavailability | **RF=3, `min.insync.replicas=2`, `acks=all`** tolerates one broker failure with no data loss and continued writes. --- ## 7.7 Retention and Log Compaction | Policy | Behavior | Use for | |---|---|---| | `cleanup.policy=delete` | Delete segments older than `retention.ms` or beyond `retention.bytes` | Event streams (e.g. 7 days) | | `cleanup.policy=compact` | Keep at least the **latest record per key**; a `null` value (**tombstone**) deletes the key | Changelogs, current-state topics, CDC, KTables | | `compact,delete` | Both | Latest state with an age limit | | **Tiered storage** (KIP-405) | Old segments offloaded to object storage | Long retention at low cost | ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Before["Before compaction"] A["k1=A | k2=B | k1=C | k3=D | k2=null | k1=E"] end subgraph After["After compaction"] B["k3=D | k1=E (k2 deleted by tombstone)"] end Before --> After ``` --- ## 7.8 Exactly-Once Semantics Kafka's EOS combines: 1. **Idempotent producer** — no duplicates from retries. 2. **Transactions** — atomically write to multiple partitions *and* commit consumer offsets (`sendOffsetsToTransaction`). 3. **`isolation.level=read_committed`** consumers — skip aborted transactional records. ```java producer.initTransactions(); while (true) { ConsumerRecords records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200)); producer.beginTransaction(); for (var r : records) { producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("invoices", r.key(), toInvoice(r.value()))); } producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(currentOffsets(records), consumer.groupMetadata()); producer.commitTransaction(); // output records + input offsets commit atomically } ``` **Scope:** consume-transform-produce **within Kafka** (Kafka Streams uses this with `processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2`). Writing to an external DB or calling an API is **not** covered — use idempotent sinks, upserts or outbox/inbox. --- ## 7.9 Retries and Dead-Letter Topics Kafka has no built-in per-message retry/DLQ (unlike RabbitMQ/SQS). Common approaches: ```mermaid flowchart LR T[orders] --> C[Consumer] C -->|fail| R1[orders.retry.1m] R1 --> RC1[Retry consumer
waits until due] RC1 -->|fail| R2[orders.retry.10m] R2 --> RC2[Retry consumer] RC2 -->|fail| DLT[orders.dlt] C -->|success| OK[commit offset] ``` | Approach | Pros | Cons | |---|---|---| | **Blocking retry** in the consumer (retry N times with backoff, then DLT) | Preserves order | Blocks the partition while retrying | | **Non-blocking retry topics** (Spring Kafka `@RetryableTopic`, Uber's pattern) | Partition keeps flowing | Breaks per-key ordering for retried records | | **Dead-letter topic** (Kafka Connect `errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name`, Spring `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer`) | Park poison records with error headers | Needs tooling to inspect and replay | --- ## 7.10 The Kafka Ecosystem | Component | Purpose | |---|---| | **Kafka Connect** | Source/sink connectors (DBs, S3, Elasticsearch…) without custom code | | **Debezium** | CDC: streams database changes (binlog/WAL) into Kafka — powers outbox relays | | **Kafka Streams** | Java library for stateful stream processing (joins, windows, aggregations, KTables) | | **ksqlDB** | SQL over streams | | **Apache Flink** | Distributed stream processing engine, widely used with Kafka | | **Schema Registry** | Avro/Protobuf/JSON Schema management with compatibility rules | | **MirrorMaker 2 / Cluster Linking** | Cross-cluster replication, DR, migration | | **Managed services** | Confluent Cloud, Amazon MSK (incl. Serverless), Aiven, Azure Event Hubs (Kafka API), Google Managed Service for Apache Kafka | | **Compatible engines** | Redpanda, WarpStream (object-storage-native), AutoMQ | --- ## 7.11 Kafka as a Message Bus vs Event Bus | Use | Fit | Notes | |---|---|---| | **Event backbone / distributed event bus** | ★★★★★ | Durable, replayable, many independent consumer groups | | **Event sourcing feed / CDC** | ★★★★☆ | Great as a transport; as the *primary* event store it lacks per-aggregate optimistic concurrency and per-entity stream reads | | **Command bus / work queue** | ★★☆☆☆ | No per-message ack, priorities, delays or routing; parallelism capped by partitions (share groups help) | | **Request/reply** | ★☆☆☆☆ | Possible (reply topics) but awkward and higher latency | --- ## 7.12 Pitfalls | Pitfall | Consequence | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Too few partitions | Can't scale consumers | Size for peak parallelism; growth plan | | Too many partitions | Metadata overhead, slower recovery | Reasonable count per broker; KRaft raises limits | | Hot keys | One partition overloaded | Better key choice, key salting (loses ordering) | | Auto-commit before processing | Message loss on crash | Manual commit after processing | | Long processing in poll loop | Exceeds `max.poll.interval.ms` → rebalance storm | Smaller batches, async processing with pause/resume | | Assuming global ordering | Bugs | Order only per partition/key | | Using Kafka for tiny-scale job queues | Operational overkill | RabbitMQ/SQS/task queue | | Unbounded schema drift | Broken consumers | Schema Registry with compatibility | --- ## 7.13 Interview Talking Points | Question | Strong answer | |---|---| | How does Kafka scale? | Topics are split into partitions spread across brokers; producers write in parallel; each consumer group divides partitions among its instances. | | How is ordering guaranteed? | Only within a partition; use a key (e.g. orderId) so related events land in the same partition. | | What happens when a consumer dies? | The group rebalances; its partitions move to other members, which resume from the last committed offset — so records after it are reprocessed (at-least-once). | | How do you avoid data loss? | RF=3, `min.insync.replicas=2`, `acks=all`, idempotent producer, unclean leader election off, commit offsets after processing. | | What is log compaction? | Retains the latest value per key (tombstones delete), turning a topic into a durable changelog of current state. | | Kafka vs RabbitMQ in one sentence? | Kafka is a replayable distributed log optimized for high-throughput event streams; RabbitMQ is a smart broker optimized for routing and per-message delivery of commands and tasks. |
keyConcepts: Kafka ecosystem: Connect, Streams, Schema Registry, Debezium

title: Service Bus Frameworks and Abstractions
bodyMd:
# 8. Service Bus Frameworks and Abstractions ## Table of Contents - [8.1 Why a Framework on Top of the Broker?](#81-why-a-framework-on-top-of-the-broker) - [8.2 What These Frameworks Provide](#82-what-these-frameworks-provide) - [8.3 .NET: MassTransit, NServiceBus, Wolverine, Brighter, Rebus](#83-net-masstransit-nservicebus-wolverine-brighter-rebus) - [8.4 Java: Spring Cloud Stream, Spring AMQP / Kafka, Axon, Apache Camel](#84-java-spring-cloud-stream-spring-amqp--kafka-axon-apache-camel) - [8.5 Polyglot / Cloud-Native: Dapr, Knative Eventing](#85-polyglot--cloud-native-dapr-knative-eventing) - [8.6 Node.js, Python and Go Options](#86-nodejs-python-and-go-options) - [8.7 In-Process Buses (Mediator Pattern)](#87-in-process-buses-mediator-pattern) - [8.8 Comparison Table](#88-comparison-table) - [8.9 Testing Message-Based Code](#89-testing-message-based-code) - [8.10 Interview Talking Points](#810-interview-talking-points) --- > **Purpose:** In real codebases "the message bus" is usually a *library* (MassTransit, NServiceBus, Spring Cloud Stream, Dapr…) wrapping a broker. Know what they give you, how they differ, and when the raw client is enough. --- ## 8.1 Why a Framework on Top of the Broker? Using a raw client (RabbitMQ.Client, `pika`, `amqplib`, Kafka clients, AWS SDK) means every team re-implements the same things: serialization, topology, retries, error queues, outbox, correlation, tracing, sagas. A **service bus framework** gives you: ```mermaid flowchart TB APP["Your handlers:
OrderPlacedConsumer"] --> FW subgraph FW["Bus framework"] direction LR S[Serialization
+ type mapping] --> R[Routing &
topology conventions] R --> RT[Retries, delayed
redelivery, DLQ] RT --> O[Outbox / Inbox] O --> SG[Sagas / state machines] SG --> OB[Tracing, metrics,
logging] end FW --> T{Transport} T --> RMQ[RabbitMQ] T --> ASB[Azure Service Bus] T --> SQS[Amazon SQS/SNS] T --> K[Kafka / Event Hubs] T --> MEM[In-memory
for tests] ``` **Key benefit — transport abstraction:** the same handler code runs over RabbitMQ locally, Azure Service Bus in production, and an in-memory transport in tests. **Cost:** another dependency (sometimes commercial), conventions to learn, and abstraction leaks (Kafka semantics differ fundamentally from queues). --- ## 8.2 What These Frameworks Provide | Capability | Description | |---|---| | **Send / Publish / Request** API | Commands to endpoints, events to subscribers, request-response | | **Convention-based topology** | Auto-create queues, exchanges/topics, subscriptions per message type | | **Message type ↔ routing** | Polymorphic routing (subscribe to an interface, receive all implementations) | | **Retry policies** | Immediate + delayed (second-level) retries with backoff | | **Error / DLQ handling** | Faulted messages moved to an error queue with exception details | | **Transactional outbox & inbox** | Atomic DB + publish, deduplication on receive | | **Sagas / process managers** | Persistent state machines correlated by ID, with timeouts | | **Scheduling** | Deferred/scheduled messages | | **Middleware pipeline** | Filters for logging, validation, auth, tenancy | | **Observability** | OpenTelemetry tracing and metrics out of the box | | **Testing harnesses** | In-memory buses and assertions on sent/published messages | --- ## 8.3 .NET: MassTransit, NServiceBus, Wolverine, Brighter, Rebus ### MassTransit - Most popular .NET service bus. Transports: RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, Amazon SQS/SNS, ActiveMQ, Kafka & Event Hubs ("Riders"), PostgreSQL/SQL Server (SQL transport), in-memory. - Features: consumers, **state-machine sagas** (Automatonymous), **Courier** routing slips, transactional outbox (EF Core, MongoDB), request client, scheduling, test harness. - **Licensing:** v8 is open source (Apache 2.0); the project announced that **v9 moves to a commercial license** (2025). Check the current terms before adopting. ```csharp public class OrderStateMachine : MassTransitStateMachine { public State Submitted { get; private set; } = null!; public State Paid { get; private set; } = null!; public Event OrderSubmitted { get; private set; } = null!; public Event PaymentCaptured { get; private set; } = null!; public OrderStateMachine() { InstanceState(x => x.CurrentState); Event(() => OrderSubmitted, e => e.CorrelateById(m => m.Message.OrderId)); Event(() => PaymentCaptured, e => e.CorrelateById(m => m.Message.OrderId)); Initially( When(OrderSubmitted) .Then(ctx => ctx.Saga.Total = ctx.Message.Total) .Send(new Uri("queue:payments"), ctx => new CapturePayment(ctx.Saga.CorrelationId, ctx.Saga.Total)) .TransitionTo(Submitted)); During(Submitted, When(PaymentCaptured) .Publish(ctx => new OrderPaid(ctx.Saga.CorrelationId)) .TransitionTo(Paid)); } } ``` ### NServiceBus (Particular Software) - Commercial, very mature, strong focus on reliability: built-in outbox, recoverability (immediate + delayed retries), sagas with timeouts, **ServicePulse/ServiceInsight** for monitoring and replaying failed messages. - Transports: RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, Amazon SQS, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Azure Storage Queues, Learning transport. ```csharp public class OrderPlacedHandler : IHandleMessages { public async Task Handle(OrderPlaced message, IMessageHandlerContext context) { await context.Send(new ChargeCustomer { OrderId = message.OrderId }); await context.Publish(new BillingStarted { OrderId = message.OrderId }); } } ``` ### Wolverine (JasperFx) - Open-source "next-gen" mediator **and** message bus in one; integrates tightly with Marten (PostgreSQL event store). Low-ceremony handlers (plain methods), durable inbox/outbox, transports for RabbitMQ, ASB, SQS, Kafka, Pulsar, local queues. ### Brighter / Rebus - **Brighter:** command processor + dispatcher, outbox/inbox, many transports (Paramore). Open source. - **Rebus:** lean, open-source service bus with a simple API; many transports. --- ## 8.4 Java: Spring Cloud Stream, Spring AMQP / Kafka, Axon, Apache Camel ### Spring Cloud Stream - Binder abstraction over RabbitMQ, Kafka, Pulsar, Solace, Kinesis, Azure Event Hubs/Service Bus, Google Pub/Sub. Functional model (`Supplier`, `Function`, `Consumer` beans) bound to destinations via config. ```java @SpringBootApplication public class BillingApp { @Bean public Consumer orderPlaced(InvoiceService invoices) { return event -> invoices.create(event.orderId(), event.total()); } } ``` ```yaml spring: cloud: stream: bindings: orderPlaced-in-0: destination: orders group: billing # consumer group → durable, load-balanced rabbit: bindings: orderPlaced-in-0: consumer: auto-bind-dlq: true republish-to-dlq: true ``` ### Spring AMQP / Spring for Apache Kafka Lower-level templates and listeners (`RabbitTemplate`, `@RabbitListener`, `KafkaTemplate`, `@KafkaListener`, `@RetryableTopic`) when you need broker-specific control. ### Axon Framework CQRS + Event Sourcing framework with command bus, event bus, query bus and sagas; Axon Server as event store and message router. ### Apache Camel Integration framework implementing the EIP catalog with hundreds of components (routing DSL: `from("rabbitmq:orders").filter(...).to("kafka:audit")`). The spiritual successor of ESB ideas, but embedded in services. --- ## 8.5 Polyglot / Cloud-Native: Dapr, Knative Eventing ### Dapr (Distributed Application Runtime) - A **sidecar** exposing building blocks over HTTP/gRPC, including **pub/sub**. The app publishes to `localhost:3500/v1.0/publish//`; Dapr talks to the configured broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis, ASB, SNS/SQS, Pub/Sub, NATS, Pulsar…). - Uses **CloudEvents** envelopes, supports at-least-once, dead-letter topics, routing rules, outbox (state store + pub/sub). - Swap brokers by changing a YAML component, without code changes. ```yaml apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1 kind: Component metadata: name: orders-pubsub spec: type: pubsub.rabbitmq version: v1 metadata: - name: connectionString value: "amqp://rabbitmq:5672" ``` ```bash curl -X POST http://localhost:3500/v1.0/publish/orders-pubsub/order-placed \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"orderId":"42"}' ``` ### Knative Eventing Kubernetes-native event mesh: **Brokers** and **Triggers** (filter on CloudEvents attributes) deliver events over HTTP to services; backed by Kafka, RabbitMQ or in-memory channels. --- ## 8.6 Node.js, Python and Go Options | Ecosystem | Libraries | Notes | |---|---|---| | **Node.js** | NestJS microservices (transports for RabbitMQ, Kafka, NATS, Redis, MQTT), BullMQ (Redis job queues), `amqplib`, KafkaJS / `@confluentinc/kafka-javascript`, Moleculer | NestJS gives decorator-based handlers (`@EventPattern`, `@MessagePattern`) | | **Python** | Celery (tasks over RabbitMQ/Redis), Dramatiq, FastStream (Kafka/RabbitMQ/NATS/Redis with Pydantic), `aio-pika`, `confluent-kafka`, Kombu | Celery is task-oriented, not an integration bus | | **Go** | Watermill (pub/sub abstraction, CQRS component, many backends), NATS client, Sarama / franz-go (Kafka) | Watermill is the closest to a Go "service bus" | ```python # FastStream example — RabbitMQ consumer and publisher with typed messages from faststream import FastStream from faststream.rabbit import RabbitBroker from pydantic import BaseModel class OrderPlaced(BaseModel): order_id: str total: float broker = RabbitBroker("amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672/") app = FastStream(broker) @broker.subscriber("billing.order-placed") @broker.publisher("billing.invoice-created") async def handle(event: OrderPlaced) -> dict: return {"order_id": event.order_id, "invoice": f"INV-{event.order_id}"} ``` --- ## 8.7 In-Process Buses (Mediator Pattern) An **in-process bus** dispatches messages to handlers inside the same process — no broker, no network. | Library | Platform | Notes | |---|---|---| | **MediatR** | .NET | `IRequest`/`IRequestHandler` (commands/queries), `INotification` (events), pipeline behaviors. Moved to a commercial license in 2025 (v13+) | | **Wolverine local queues** | .NET | Same API locally and over transports; durable local queues | | **Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher`** | Java | `@EventListener`, `@TransactionalEventListener` (fire after commit) | | **Guava EventBus** | Java | Simple annotation-based pub/sub (Guava docs now recommend alternatives) | | **Node `EventEmitter`** | Node.js | Built-in event emitter; synchronous listeners | | **NestJS CQRS** | Node.js | `CommandBus`, `QueryBus`, `EventBus` | **When useful:** modular monoliths, separating command/query handlers (CQRS), cross-cutting pipelines (validation, logging, transactions). **Caveat:** an in-process bus gives *code* decoupling, not *runtime* decoupling — if the process crashes, in-flight messages are gone unless you add a durable outbox/local queue. --- ## 8.8 Comparison Table | Framework | Language | License | Transports | Sagas | Outbox | Notable | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | **MassTransit** | .NET | v8 Apache 2.0, v9 commercial | RabbitMQ, ASB, SQS, ActiveMQ, Kafka, SQL, in-memory | ✅ state machines | ✅ | Huge community, test harness | | **NServiceBus** | .NET | Commercial | RabbitMQ, ASB, SQS, SQL, PostgreSQL | ✅ | ✅ | Ops tooling (ServicePulse), support | | **Wolverine** | .NET | MIT | RabbitMQ, ASB, SQS, Kafka, Pulsar, local | ✅ | ✅ | Mediator + bus, Marten integration | | **Brighter** | .NET | MIT | RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS, ASB, Redis… | ❌ (process managers by hand) | ✅ | Command processor | | **Spring Cloud Stream** | Java | Apache 2.0 | RabbitMQ, Kafka, Pulsar, cloud binders | ❌ | Via Spring Modulith/Debezium | Functional binding model | | **Axon** | Java | Apache 2.0 (Server: commercial tiers) | Axon Server, Kafka, AMQP | ✅ | N/A (event store) | CQRS/ES-first | | **Apache Camel** | Java | Apache 2.0 | 300+ components | ✅ (Saga EIP) | Partial | EIP routing DSL | | **Dapr** | Any (sidecar) | Apache 2.0 | 15+ brokers | Workflows building block | ✅ | Broker portability, CloudEvents | | **Watermill** | Go | MIT | Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, SQL, Pub/Sub… | ❌ | ✅ (forwarder) | CQRS component | | **NestJS microservices** | TS | MIT | RabbitMQ, Kafka, NATS, Redis, MQTT, gRPC | ❌ | ❌ | Decorator-based | --- ## 8.9 Testing Message-Based Code | Level | Approach | |---|---| | **Unit** | Call the handler directly with a message; assert side effects and messages sent (frameworks provide fake contexts) | | **Component** | In-memory transport / test harness (MassTransit `ITestHarness`, NServiceBus testing, Spring `TestChannelBinder`) | | **Integration** | Real broker in **Testcontainers** (RabbitMQ, Kafka, LocalStack for SQS/SNS, Azure Service Bus emulator) | | **Contract** | Pact message pacts or schema registry compatibility checks | | **End-to-end** | Poll/await eventual outcomes with timeouts (`Awaitility`, polling helpers); avoid fixed sleeps | ```csharp [Test] public async Task Publishes_OrderSubmitted_when_SubmitOrder_is_consumed() { await using var provider = new ServiceCollection() .AddMassTransitTestHarness(x => x.AddConsumer()) .AddSingleton() .BuildServiceProvider(true); var harness = provider.GetRequiredService(); await harness.Start(); await harness.Bus.Publish(new SubmitOrder(Guid.NewGuid(), "c-1", 10m)); Assert.That(await harness.Consumed.Any()); Assert.That(await harness.Published.Any()); } ``` --- ## 8.10 Interview Talking Points | Question | Strong answer | |---|---| | Why use MassTransit/NServiceBus instead of the RabbitMQ client? | They standardize topology, serialization, retries, error queues, outbox, sagas, tracing and testing, and abstract the transport so you can switch brokers. | | Downside of these abstractions? | Extra dependency and licensing, hidden topology, and leaky abstractions — log-based transports (Kafka) don't behave like queues. | | What is Dapr pub/sub? | A sidecar API for publish/subscribe using CloudEvents, where the broker is a pluggable component configured in YAML. | | MediatR vs a message bus? | MediatR is an in-process mediator: code-level decoupling, no durability or cross-process delivery. A message bus crosses process boundaries through a durable broker. | | How do you test message handlers? | Unit-test handlers directly, use in-memory harnesses for component tests, Testcontainers for broker integration, and contract tests for message schemas. |
keyConcepts: service bus frameworks vs raw broker clients
